He said: For the information of hon. members I beg to submit the following general notes of interest:
(1)	The return covers all permits issued between the 19th July and the 31st December, 1924. The 19th July was the date upon which the amendment to section 4 of the Immigration Act became law.
(2)	In several cases it will be observed that a permit was issued in cases where deportation had been ordered. In this connection it is well to recognize that where complaint is made to the department with a view to deportation and the board of inquiry finds that the

person is deportable, the deportation order is issued . as a matter of course. Provision is made in the law for an appeal to the minister. In a number of cases consideration has been shown on appeal. If the person whose deportation was ordered were allowed to continue residence in Canada without being placed under permit, that person, on the completion of five years' stay in Canada, would acquire Canadian domicile and could not then be deported. The issue of the permit automatically lifts such person out of the immigrant class and places him in the nonimmigrant class and prevents time running in his favour for the acquisition of domicile. This explains why permits are sometimes issued in deportation cases.

I desire to offer a few remarks upon the resolution and amendment which are now before the House. There are two important factors in the life of Canada, and in fact in almost every other country, but more especially in this country of wide distances and long hauls in the matter of transportation. The first question to which I refer is that of production, and the second, that of transportation and distribution. I do not intend at this time to take up any of the time of the House in dealing with the question of production. As regards distribution, however, I may say just in

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
That was 1913. I am reading these extracts to show that there have existed in the past conditions very similar to those which we are considering at the present time, and that numerous demands have been made at various times that the problem should be dealt with. Apparently everybody so far has recognized the existence of the evil. In 1914 the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) was sent to England to look into the matter, and after considerable investigation he appeared to be very much disappointed with the outlook. He came back, and nothing was done at that time. In 1918 the Dominions Royal Commission reported there there existed a combine of ship owners operating against the public interest and that a discrimination in rates was being practised against Great Britain in favour of foreign countries. Sir George Perley also wrote that rates "during past years" had been higher than were reasonable; and Sir Thomas White cabled to the High Commissioner for Canada that he was much concerned about freight rates and was anxious to have inquiries made in Great Britain to ascertain whether anything could be done in the way of co-operation.
We can see therefore that attempts have been made from time to time to deal with what apparently has been regarded as an evil by different governments and different members of those governments during a number of years past. Whatever may be the facts, everyone knows beyond question that rates have increased most enormously since this conference, or combine, or whatever you ehoose to call it, has come into existence.
In this connection let me say just a few words touching the Preston report. I do not think it is at all necessary that we should pay very much attention to that report; I do not see that we need take up the time of the House discussing it so far as the question of transportation and ocean rates is concerned. It seems to me that the fact has been fully acknowledged by different governments and by former members of this government that freight fates have been uniformly higher than they ought to be; that would appear to be established even apart from the evidence that has been submitted in the Preston report. Now, I have nothing to do with the personality of Mr. Preston, about whom I really do not know very much; and so far as I can see, that does not enter into the matter at all. If Mr. Preston is presenting the facts as they are, the facts will stand investigation independently of what we may think of Mr. Preston; and if they are not facts but only unfounded allegations they will fall to the ground. It is a very common practice in law, although I am not so sure of this, not having any knowledge of courts and lawyers, that when a lawyer has no case the best thing for him to do is to abuse opposing counsel in order to fill up the time and show at any rate that he has something to say. And while this abuse of Mr. Preston may be necessary under certain circumstances, to my mind at Jeast it has very little to do with the question under consideration; the facts which Mr. Preston has submitted are what we have to Consider at the present time. Are the statements made by Mr. Preston borne out by the facts as they are? That is what we have to consider now, that is the extent to which we must take his report into consideration. No doubt it may turn out that Mr. Preston has attempted to prove too much; and it seems to me on the face of the report that sometimes it might have been better if he had stated the case a little more mildly. Had he done so he would perhaps have re-
Ocean Shipping Rates

ceived a little more attention and been more readily believed1. At the same time, I am not disposed, as some members of this House are, to discount the report. It is possible that the statements contained in it may be proved to be not so very far astray after all.
We are met however by a straight denial on the part of the steamship companies of some of the facts stated in the report. We have Sir William Noble of the Cunard line making the statement that any action by this House to take into consideration some of the allegations made might well alienate the sympathy of the steamship companies. This is a serious state of affairs indeed, and I would call the attention of hon. members to the threat; the very fact that this House should attempt to investigate the proceedings of the combine will "alienate the sympathy" of the steamship companies from the people of the country! Well, I do not think for one moment that these steamship companies are in the business for their health or for the benefit of the people: they are in the business for what they can make out of it. I am not afraid therefore that we shall lose their sympathy or that any damage will accrue from any investigation we may make into the manner in which these companies carry on their business.
I want to say now a few words about the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and before proceeding I would read a short extract from the Ottawa Journal. I read this paragraph to refresh my own memory and those of other hon. gentlemen:
If the King government thinks an Atlantic combine exists, let it use and subsidize its own ships to fight it. Canada to-day has a merchant marine of 57 fine ships. Two of them are of gross tonnage exceeding 7,000; twenty-three of tonnage over 5,000; one of tonnage over 4,000; fifteen of tonnage over 3,000; fifteen of tonnage over 2,000; and one of 1,766 tonnage.
Their total tonnage is, roughly, 220,000 or 125,000 tons more than the ships to be provided by Petersen. What a farce, therefore, to have this Canadian government tonnage with insufficient cargoes or rusting at docks, while proposing to bonus an outsider with millions for fewer and no better ships?
That does seem a rather serious charge to bring against the government under the conditions that now exist; but we want to get all the information we can regarding the Canadian Government Merchant Marine before passing judgment. I listened with a good deal of pleasure to the speech delivered the other day by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) in the course of which he discussed the question of shipping. Perhaps that hon. gentleman is more fully informed on this subject than any other hon. member who sits on this side. Unfortunately, however, I was unable to be present during the delivery

of another speech, that of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) which the House heard yesterday afternoon, and as I have not been able to read his speech in Hansard I have not the benefit of his remarks on the subject. I consider the hon. member better informed on shipping matters than most of the hon. gentlemen that sit on his side, and for that reason I regret not being in possession of the facts he submitted. However, I have several statements in regard to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine which I should like to read.

Another memorandum prepared by the Deputy Minister of Agriculture states:
It has been contended that smaller boats were not suitable lor the cattle trade. This is demonstrated by the serious loss of cattle from the Commander in October. 1921, when she lost 57 head from a load of 280 cattle.
The following extract is hardly along the same line, but I think it will be interesting to hon. members. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) stated):
If the Canadian Government Merchant Marine were not in the conference they might get cargoes east, but for a cargo to come west they would have to compete with the entire North Atlantic Steamship Conference, and would come back empty.
This correspondence in connection with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is not very encouraging. During the four sessions I have been in this House I have listened to a good many discussions regarding our fleet, Mr. Speaker, and I have not yet been able to determine just exactly what traffic the ships are suited for. I think it is about time we decided whether we have something that is of value to the country in transporting our products overseas, or whether our merchant marine is always going to be a liability. Of course, I realize that the boats were built at a time when shipbuilding costs were very high, and that consequently we may have no reason to expe'Cft any return upon the capital expenditure, but it seems to me it would be well for us to ascertain just
exactly what traffic these boats are suitable for and utilize them accordingly, so that they may earn at least enough to pay operating expenses. It is very unfortunate that the present condition should be allowed to continue. I shall refer to this subject again when dealing with the Petersen contract.
Turning again to the cattle trade: I have not the exact year, but the year previous to the passing of the Fordney tariff by Congress,
I find we exported to the United States 500,000 head of cattle; in 1923 our exportation dropped to 65,629 head; that same year we exported to Great Britain 39,856 head. So our total exportation for 1923 was something like 105,000 head, against 500,000 exported to the United States alone before the Fordney tariff went into effect, showing what a tremendous blow that was to our cattle industry. However, we have no reason to complain against the action of the United States government; if they saw fit to erect a tariff barrier against our cattle, while it was a serious blow to Canadian stockmen, yet it was the United States' own business, and we have to find another market to take our surplus cattle. That is why it is so important that transportation rates both on land and sea should be as low as possible in order that we may reach the markets of the Old Country. During the last few years, I find there has been a very serious increase in rates to Great Britain. From 1904 to 1912 the ocean freight rate was less than $8 per head. At that time the rail rate from Winnipeg to Montreal was $7.26, and the ocean rate thence to Liverpool $7.30

a difference of only 4 cents. Last year the rail rate from Winnipeg to Montreal was $10.20, while the ocean rate to Liverpool had increased to $20. This is something I have considerable difficulty in understanding, although there may be satisfactory explanation from the shipping companies. No one in this House will contend for a moment that railway operating costs have not, increased enormously duriug the last few years-wages, materials and equipment have increased very greatly since pre-war days

and yet we find that although from 1904 to 1912 the freight rate from Winnipeg to Montreal and the ocean rate from Montreal to Liverpool were nearly the same, today the railways carry cattle from Winnipeg to Montreal for about one-half what the shipping companies charge to transport them to Liverpool. Now then, why has the ocean transportation charge increased so tremendously as against the comparatively moderate increase in railway transportation charge during the past few years? So far I have never
Ocean Shipping Rates

received any adequate explanation for this great disparity.
At this time the question naturally arises: If there is a combine, will the proposal contained in the resolution offer a satisfactory solution? I wish I was able to answer the question offhand. But I do not know. However. it is worth considering. We have seen that the high cost of ocean transportation from Canada to Europe has for a number of years caused a great deal of disquietude to those who have had control of the administration of this country, but unfortunately all the activities that have taken place from time to time have brought no benefit to our exporters and importers, and consequently it is about time we woke up and tried to do something to remedy this unsatisfactory state of affairs. I am not prepared to endorse offhand the proposal contained in this resolution. I am aware that a great many objection^ can be urged against some of 'the details, and of course we expect that whatever attempt is made to combat any conference or combine will meet with the most strenuous opposition from those interested in the continuation of high ocean rates. We can well understand that the government is undertaking something that entails upon it a tremendous responsibility. If this parliament undertakes to fight a combination so wide in its extent as the North Atlantic Steamship Conference it is undertaking a pretty heavy task and will have a bitter fight on its hands. At the same time I do not feel like giving up and saying we can do nothing. I do not think we should fold our hands and say, "We will let matters take their course and everything will come right in the end."
I do not wish in any way to reflect upon the British government, but I saw a statement in the British press not long ago to the effect that Sir William Petersen will be able to get no assistance in the way of financing from the Trade Facilities Act of Great Britain. Then, I noticed a reference in the Morning Post-a very respectable paper, Mr. Speaker, as everyone knows who knows anything about British newspapers; a paper which, I am sure, would not look with any degree of encouragement upon any such proposal as that which is now before this House-says:
This arrangement is a sinister attack upon the unity of the Empire.
Just think of it; the idea that any parliament would dare to investigate such an arrangement as is supposed to exist in connection with the north Atlantic shipping combine! It makes me just a little suspicious when the Morning Post takes up the FMr. Forke.]
cudgels on behalf of that conference and claims that any criticism of their conduct is an attack upon the unity of the empire. It is also stated-I do not know what truth there is in it-that the large financial interests are not too friendly to the move that has been made by the present government.
Be that as it may, we cannot an-4 p.m. ticipate that in connection with this matter the government will get much assistance from that source.
A good deal of criticism has been levelled against this proposal, and I could myself, I think, point out the inadequacy of the attempt being made by the government to fight such a large combination. I would almost be inclined to give up in despair; to believe that anjr attempt in this direction would be futile, that nothing could be accomplished against the large interests concerned. But it is interesting to note the effort that is being made to refute the charges levelled against the north Atlantic shipping conference. Gentlemen connected with these companies are waxing eloquent and going to a great deal of trouble to explain how vicious and how wrong this movement really is and 'to state that there is no ground whatever for any of the allegations made respecting high freight rates. Well, I cannot understand why they should bother themselves very much about this matter if the step which it is proposed to take could have no effect whatever upon future conditions with respect to ocean transport.

speechtext:
I cannot see the reason for all the fuss, if there is nothing in it. An hon. member to my right-I do not know who it was-made a reference the other day which seemed to indicate that there was a connection between a wheat pool and a combine; at least he suggested that a pool was in the nature of a combine. I am willing ts admit that to some extent it is, but if you will allow a momentary digression, Mr. Speaker, I will try to explain the difference between a pool such as is operated in connection with the marketing of wheat, and a combine for the raising of prices or for any other purpose. A pool has never been undertaken for the purpose of raising prices. Last fall it was stated in the public press that the pool in wheat was responsible for raising the price of wheat during the last few months. I do not for a moment agree with that view; I do not think any pool can raise the price of wheat. The idea of a pool in the marketing of wheat is this: The wheat is threshed in large

Ocean Shipping Rates
quantities and then marketed during the period from the middle of September to perhaps the middle of December. It is thrown upon the market all at once, in enormous quantities. The millers can use only certain quantities of wheat at a time, and as a rule they buy the wheat just when they want to use it. Consequently someone has to step into the market and buy the large surplus of wheat that is thrown upon it at that time. Naturally the man who buys that wheat has to speculate upon what the price will be in the future. He has to take into consideration the tying up of his money for that period, and he is not likely to take any chances; he is not likeiy to pay the highest price. The idea of a pool is to put the wheat on the market, not all at one time but just when it is required by those who are using it for milling purposes -to feed the market according to the requirements of the millers, thus bringing into action the law of supply and demand. The result is that it is quite possible for the producer to get a better price, and the consumer does not have to pay any more for the wheat than he would have paid otherwise. That also eliminates the speculator who would come between the producer and the miller who buys the wheat for grinding purposes. That is the difference I would make between a pool and a combination that can be used to enhance prices.
I do not think the members in this part of the House have ever been enamoured of subsidies. The experience of Canada in the matter of subsidies has not been a pleasant one. There is even now before the House a matter affecting a large corporation which has received an enormous amount of money from this country in subsidies. I have no hesitation in saying that it is a blot upon the fair name of this Dominion; it is a festering spot, and I am sure every loyal Canadian is ashamed of the conditions which have been brought about under the guidance of that corporation. That condition has not the effect of making us fall in love with the idea of paying large subsidies to any corporation. However, if it can be shown that a subsidy will be of real benefit I do not think I would be wedded to any particular course simply because it was an academic consideration. We are living in a practical age; we have certain conditions to face and we must meet those conditions as best we can. As to the subsidy that is proposed in this case, whatever may be said for or against it, it is for no particular class, for no particular people. If in the interests of any, it would be spent in the interests of all the people. I think, perhaps, the class
of shippers who would most benefit by a reduction in ocean freights through this special arrangement which the government is trying to make with the Petersen interests would be the package shippers.
I have suggested that the remedy that is being offered seems to me almost inadequate to meet the situation. I am told that nearly one thousand boats cleared from the harbour of Montreal during the last season; and in that connection I am quite willing to accept the figures of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who pointed out how many trips the ten boats of the Petersen company could make during the season. It does seem to me that it is almost too small to make any particular dent in the arrangements that now exist with respect to ocean shipments. However, I am quite willing to investigate this matter; I am willing to give the government the credit for at least making an attempt to do something to better the existing conditions. I know very well what the feeling would be to-day in western Canada-speaking for myself and also, probably for most of the members who are with me on this side of the House-if it were to go out that we were against any attempt to meet the existing conditions and to deal with this conference, if we were simply to lie down and say that nothing could dedone. We are anxious and Willing that some investigation should be made; and I feel perfectly certain, if this matter goes before a committee, if we can get a proper investigation such as we ought to get-the privilege of summoning witnesses and of putting them on the witness stand under oath- that whatever comes of it we will at least be in a position to know something of the facts of the case. Then, knowing the facts of the case, having got all the information we possibly can-and I think the Prime Minister has made the promise that no obstacles will be put in the way of getting the fullest possible explanation in regard to the whole affair- being in possession of all the facts of the case, we shall then be in a position to vote intelligently upon the matter. I do not want to stand up here and assume a hostile attitude in regard to this arrangement although I may be somewhat critical, because it seems to me that we are up against a proposition that is tremendously big and that we may have some difficulty in combating it. However, I would say let us make an attempt to deal with the matter anyway; let us have an investigation and find out what we can. Having done that I think most hon. members will be enabled to give an intelligent vote when the proper time comes.

Mr. Speaker, everyone must regard the situation with which we are confronted in this country as a very serious one indeed. The difficulties with which the government have to contend at this stage in our career are also very great. A number of years ago we became responsible for heavy liabilities which are increasing as the years go by. The war undoubtedly entailed many obligations. The conditions which prevail to-day, seven years after the close of the war, are not at all satisfactory, and the outlook is not at all encouraging. Therefore it behooves every loyal and patriotic citizen of Canada to do everything possible to bring about a better state of affairs. The country has great resources, many of them as yet untouched. We are in a very fortunate position in having a cjuntry so richly endowed by nature. Nevertheless the responsibilities which devolve upon us are such as to demand our most serious attention. I can assure the government that anything I may say this afternoon will not be said with any idea of embarrassing them in any way; I shall be influenced by the belief that frankness of speech is what the situation demands.
I do not feel like allowing a vote to be taken on this question without expressing my own views with respect to it. We have heard a great deal about the solution now proposed by the government for some of our difficulties embodied in the Petersen contract. Transportation, is of necessity bound to have an important influence in connection with the problems of a country so vast as is Canada. Ocean transportation is of special importance owing to our great agricultural production and the need of finding a market abroad for veay much of our bulky surplus [product. It has been said, and I think truly, that we have provided railway facilities in advance of the times; and one of our great problems to-day is to know what we are to do with such a great railway mileage throughout the country in view of our sparse population. I am not sure but that it would be wisdom on our part to close up many of the existing railways and eliminate the existing competition for traffic by some arrangement between the government railway system and the Canadian Pacific Railway There is nothing to be gained by an attempt at competition such as we witness every night in the trains which pass out of this, the capital city a/nd elsewhere. We see one train lined up on the tracks of the Canadian Pacific Railway and another on the tracks of the Canadian National, both westward bound, competing with each other for

traffic, both leaving at approximately the same time. It would be much more in the public interest if one would leave several hours in advance of the other, or, better still, if this competition could be lessened. This kind of rivalry for traffic and not in service in the same territory does not appear to me to be good business. I know the Minister of Railways is conscious of the difficulties which underlie a solution of this problem; but the need is so great that even he must be convinced that something will have to be done soon to bring about a better condition of affairs.
The contract with Sir William Petersen now before the House must have been a great surprise to the people when it was [announced. Announcement has been, made in the past of other projects which might be compared to the present one. Hon. gentlemen will recall the announcement in 1903 or 1904 of the determination to build the Transcontinental railway. The people were repeatedly informed that the actual cost in cash to them of that project would not exceed thirteen or fourteen million dollars at the outside. This was the estimate of the total cost of the enters prise to the country which was given to the public, and a great many, people in Canada accepted the statement. Now when we look back-not so very far back because twenty years is not a very long period in the life of a country-what do we find? Was the cost to the country of that railway confined to thirteen or fourteen million dollars? No, but a debt of half a billion dollars has been placed upon the shoulders of our people as a result of the carrying out of this much vaunted project which dazzled the imagination of many people twenty years ago. We should not forget facts such as this when we are asked to commit ourselves to an undertaking such as the government has now placed before us. An analysis of the arrangement as dose and as keen as is possible will therefore be in the public interest because under the circumstances in which we now find ourselves we cannot afford to experiment with any proposition which is in any way open to doubt. Before committing ourselves to such an enterprise we must be reasonably assured that the expenditure sought will accomplish the results which its promoters claim.
That being the case I wish to point out the steps which have been taken by the government in order to arrive at a solution of this matter. Two years ago a special committee of this House was appointed to inquire into agricultural conditions. Nineteen members

It appears a meeting of the committee was held when this fifth report on ocean rates was brought before the committee on a Monday morning, the 18th June. Parliament prorogued about a week afterwards. A fourth report was submitted and adopted on the morning of Monday April 23, when this matter was referred to in a general way. So far as the fifth report on ocean rates was concerned, I never saw it and never heard of it until it was printed after the prorogation of parliament. I was not present at the meeting at which it was passed. It was called on a Monday morning, near the end of the session, and that may account for my absence. I did attempt to attend the meetings of the committee as well as I could. During that session I was a member of another committee in connection with redistribution, and it was impossible for me to always attend both committees. In the seventh and last report of this committee, to which I referred last night, when the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duffl weis speaking, hon. members will find that the committee admitted the impossibility of digesting the evidence which was taken before the committee in the time at their disposal. In this their last report they say: Your committee have held eighty sittings on forty-five separate days, have heard the evidence of one hundred and three witnesses and have had two hundred and twenty-three exhibits filed with them; but have not been able to make a complete inquiry into the matters submitted to them under the order of reference.
In view of the important and widespread information collected during the sittings of your committee and the impossibility of digesting and properly weighing the evidence in the time at their disposal before prorogation, your committee respectfully recommend that a similar committee be appointed at an early period of the next session of parliament.
This resolution was carried and is the last report of this committee, from which you will see that the committee did not deal with the evidence obtained except in a general way that could not be considered as final. The view of the committee was that a similar committee should be appointed at the following session. What happened at the following session? Did the government act on the report of this committee? Did they appoint a similar committee? During the following session were they anxious that this evidence which had been obtained should be analyzed, supplemented and made available in concrete form for the members of the House? No; they allowed the session to pass without anything being done in that regard. I have one volume here containing the evidence, and there is another volume as large as this one, containing somewhere in the neighbourhood of twenty-two hundred pages of evidence and other matter. The committee was appointed to investigate agricultural conditions. But what about the question of transportation? Transportation might be connected, and undoubtedly is vitally connected, with agricultural conditions. But this committee was appointed for the purpose of investigating agricultural conditions; and while it is true they did devote considerable attention to railway and ocean transportation, there was nothing final or conclusive in what they did in their respect.

But, nothwithstanding all protests and the motion I moved in this House, this man was selected and his report, bearing date December 31, 1924, has been submitted to parliament. The contract with Sir William Petersen which is now under consideration was made twenty days before the Preston report was submitted. I noticed in the Manitoba Free Press, a few days ago an intimation that the contract was entered into during the summer-quite a long time ago. This journal says:
As to Sir William Petersen, his difficulties seem to be the result of the change in government which took place in England last autumn. The contract with the Canadian government was entered into in the summer when the government of Ramsay MacDonald was in power. The Labour party in England received Sir William's overtures for assistance in very friendly fashion, and it is said he had arranged for an advance under the Trade Facilities Act before the contract was signed.
Surely the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), instead of assuming a defiant attitude when addressing the. House on this question might have been frank in his statement, and I am confident, if he had, a good deal of this discussion would have been avoided. But he pursued the very unusual course of stating that the government were not accepting responsibility for the contract, although he said it was a cast-iron one. Cast-iron is not a very flexible commodity, you cannot make any impression on it by squeezing, you oannot pare it; you can only alter it by breaking it. The minister stated he was going to ask that this cast-iron contract should be submitted to a special committee of this House. It is most unusual for a government to submit their policy to a special committee and be unable to alter it if deemed advisable. I do not think any hon. member has ever heard of such a proceeding before. My hon. friends to the left may say, "Oh, but this is the democratic way of doing things." Well, it may be democratic according to their views, but I venture to say that it is not in accordance with British parliamentary practice and procedure. All that this contract lacks is the ratification of parliament. Having entered into the contract, why do the government not assume full responsibility, submit it to the committee of

Does the minister not know, do the government not know, what arguments they have to advance to justify the ratification of this contract by the House? Is It necessary to inform the House through a special committee, to call witnesses before tihat special committee, and then put all the other members of this House to the trouble of seeking information from the members of the special committee? It has always been customary in the British parliament to place the fullest information on any subject before the people's representatives. But it is significant that the government have apparently abandoned the W. T. R. Preston report, and they are not today even relying on the report of the special committee of two sessions ago, on agricultural conditions, for the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) last night took great care in the latter part of his address to point out that the contract was entered into as the result of some other information which the government had obtained, not because of any information they derived from those sources first referred to. Then if conditions such as those referred to in the Manitoba Free Press and elsewhere are responsible for a change in the contract, let the government make a new contract with Sir William Petersen, if necessary, and submit it to the House in the usual way. speechtext:
He will not require even
the help of the able Minister of Agriculture. The hon. member for South Oxford read a letter purporting to 'be written by Mr. Preston in reference to the distribution of votes of immigrants. It sounds almost like a page out .of the War-time Elections Act when, by legislation, the votes of our boys were partitioned out through the Dominion of Canada where they would do the most good to the Tory party. What Mr. Preston, even if the letter be correct, said in that letter, is not a circumstance to what was done in the Wartime Elections Act. The letter was the opinion of one man, while t'he degradation of the electorate of Canada was the combined effort and concerted legislation of a party. I am through with my hon. friend.
This question of transportation, of course, as all hon. members know, is a difficult one and not a new one. I often think, sitting quietly, that the reasons for some of the difficulties of industry, particularly agriculture, are deeper even than transportation, with this explanation only, that exorbitant cost of transportation is one of the nibblers at the success of the agricultural industry. Hon. members have all noticed, when a man brings to town a load of hay, not pressed, just in the ordinary old hayrack, loose, with a binder on top, that every hungry horse along the road takes a nibble at the load of hay. There are people who are sufficiently charitable to their horses and uncharitable to the man who is selling the hay to drive up a team and let them eat at it all along the road. It just strikes me that a comparison can be made there with the different processes that are nibbling at the products of the farm, the mine, the forest and the fisheries from the time those products leave the hands of the producer until they get into the hands of the consumer. In years gone by our great grandfathers took a bag of grain in on horseback to the old-fashioned mill and got back a certain quantity of flour and a certain quantity of the by-product. It was said even then that our friends the millers took quite a bit of toll. A little later the wheat was drawn in and ground and flour taken home with a team-a little advancement. Up to that time
there was only one toll. Following that, the wheat was drawn into town and was traded for flour-two tolls. Later on the wheat was brought in and sold and the money was used to buy the flour-another toll added-middlemen in different capacities. This has now reached the point they tell me that when many of our good friends take their wheat into town, they take home not flour, but bread. So that everyone gets a crack at this load of wheat before it reaches its destination. I am taking wheat as an example. Let us follow it from the time it leaves the home of the producer; elevator, percentage; out of the elevator on to the train, percentage; Winnipeg sale, percentage, broker; down to the ship on the Great Lakes, broker; insurance, broker. So that by the time you have got it over the ocean and have paid the freight rates you have paid out a lot in percentages; and when you want to sell the grain finally there is another broker to be considered. I have come to the conclusion therefore that the great trouble with our trade in Canada-and probably it is the same in other countries- is that we have not yet solved the problem of getting the product of the producer to the home of the consumer without incurring a great deal of expense in the transition.

speechtext: We are getting there out in the west.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I was going to refer to
that. You have a wheat pool in the west which has been accomplishing a good deal. But after a visit to Europe, after you have seen what Australia and other countries are doing, you must admit that the wheat pool solves the difficulty only at one end of the route; and in my humble judgment there should be some way by which the Liverpool, the Antwerp, the Hamburg market, and the prices which the farmer gets in the west might be more comparable than they are at the present time. We send our product over there; we have several associations all doing good work. But that product has to be handled through another process of brokerage, or whatever you may call it, before it is really sold to the consumer. The same thing applies in a measure to flour, perhaps in as great a measure. This is only a hint I throw out before coming to the discussion of ocean freight rates, because ocean freight rates form one incident, and a not inconsiderable one, of the-taxes that are placed on the products of Canada, as of other countries, from the time they come from the soil until they reach the home of the consumer.
In 1903 the question of freight rates by land was taken up in a very practical way,
Ocean Shipping Rates

and what is known as the Board of Railway Commissioners was appointed. Before that time everything depended on the state of mind of the railway companies as well as on t'he extent of competition. I am a full believer in the work done by the Board of Railway Commissioners, and I believe that we should have been in a much more chaotic state in this country had we not had some authority to which to refer our railway problems. The United States has had an interstate board with, I believe, less authority perhaps than is the case in Canada. They have problems which perhaps are more difficult to solve than ours owing to the fact that their state incorporation and control of railways in the various states is more marked than is our provincial control; for although it is not here a matter of statute, it has become largely a matter of practice that steam roads should be under the Board of Railway Commissioners. But after the Board of Railway Commissioners had settled down to work and had established a basis of rates, the people discovered that no matter how fair a rate might be by land, say from the west to the east or vice versa, it was within the power of the ship owners by increasing rates on the ocean, to nullify all benefits the people might receive by a reduction in the cost of land carriage. For example, if one company owned a railway and a steamship line as well, it made no difference very materially to that company where the rates were placed on land, so long as they could place the rates on the ocean at a point that would make up for all that they lost in railway carriage. And what was applicable to companies owning both a railway and a steamship line was applicable generally, inasmuch as other railways would have traffic arrangements with ocean vessels, by which the two carrying systems could so adjust their rates that, no matter how you might control the land rate, the ocean rate could be so fixed as to wipe out any benefit that the shippers might otherwise receive.
That was found to be the case; at least that was the situation in 1010. In that year I had the privilege of taking up this question of ocean freight rates with the then chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the late Mr. Justice Mabee. Anyone who knew Mr. Justice Mabee and knew of his work as head of the railway board will agree with me that he was a strong friend of the public, and endeavoured to render decisions which, while not being unfair to the companies, would at the same time afford all the relief possible to shippers. I am going to quote at some length from a memorandum prepared by Mr. Justice Mabee on this ques-

tion, because I want to make it clear that the statement that this subject of ocean freight rates is new is not by any means correct. The problem has been wrestled with by governments for the last fifteen years, but this is the only government that has had courage enough to tackle it. This memorandum was prepared by Mr. Justice Mabee at my request and forwarded to the British government, and I shall read it because I believe it contains information which, coming from a man like him, will be of deep interest to the shipping public and to every bon. member of this House. On February 18, 1910, I wrote the following letter to the present Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) then Secretary of State:
Dear Mr. Murphy:
I enclose a memo made by the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, at my request, in reference to joint action between the government of Great Britain and the government of Canada respecting the regulation of ocean rates.
Will you kindly bring this to the attention of the home government, so that consultation might be had on the subject, as I deem it very desirable that steps should be taken to control these rates, for reasons which are set out in the memo.
Yours truly,
Geo. P. Graham.
Hon. Charles Murphy, M.P.,
Secretary of State.
The memorandum in question is as follows:
Memorandum showing the necessity for legislative control over ocean rates and facilities between Great Britain and Canada.
For many years in England, in the United States and in Canada, the principle of governmental control over railway rates and facilities has been in active operation. These countries found it necessary, in the interest of the public, to establish tribunals with statutory authority to control the rates or tolls that railway companies charge the public for the carriage of traffic. The legislation in the three countries differs in detail, but the English act forms the basis of the others; the tribunals have different names, their jurisdictions vary in many details, some having wider powers over a greater majority of subjects than others, but over the control of freight and passenger rates upon railways there is a common field of jurisdiction.
In Canada the Board of Railway Commissioners has under the various acts affecting it, namely, 3 Ed. VII, Cap. 37. 6 & 7 Ed. VII, Cap. 38, 7 & 8 Ed. VII, Cap. 61 & 62, 8 & 9 Ed. VII, Cap. 31 & 32, jurisdiction over almost all matters relating to railways (except incorporations), as well as telegraph, telephone and express companies.
The jurisdiction of all these controlling bodies is limited to the land, or land and inland water movement; in other words, the moment that export traffic reaches the seaboard of any of these three countries, government control over its movement is entirely lost.
First, as to the existing conditions regarding the transportation of traffic from Canada to Great Britain; take the shipment of grain from Winnipeg to Liverpool via Montreal and the St. Lawrence route. The all rail haul from Winnipeg to Montreal is 1,414 miles; the distance from there to Liverpool via Belle Isle is 2,760 miles, and via Cape Race, 3,007 miles.

Ocean Shipping Rates
Under the present law, when these shipments reach Montreal, control over the rates and conditions of transportation is lost, the result being that for two-thirds of the total distance the traffic moves at the rates the ocean carriers choose to make. If this grain moves from Winnipeg via Fort William or Port Arthur to Georgian bay ports, and thence rail to Montreal, the inland movement is some 200 miles shorter and control over the through shipment that much less.
If it is wise to control the transportation upon land, why is it not in principle equally wise and in the public interest to control the ocean movement? If the public derives any benefit from the control of the rates affecting the land movement of the above traffic, that being one-third of the distance, it is fair to assume that it would derive much greater benefit if the rates from Winnipeg all the way to Liverpool were under control.
In this connection it may be noted that the government has expended nearly $11,000,000 on the St. Lawrence ship channel; over $1,000,000 on the Montreal harbour; has loaned nearly $11,000,000 to the commissioners of the Montreal Harbour Board; and has large annual outlays for lighting and buoying the St. Lawrence route, and all these expenditures have been and are being made that the cost of carriage along the St. Lawrence route may be cheapened by the elimination of the dangers of navigation. In the last annual report of the Montreal harbour commissioners, it is stated that the St. Lawrence river from the ocean to Montreal is acknowledged to be the best lighted and buoyed ship channel in the world.
It is said that some $750,000 has already been expended upon surveys for the Georgian bay ship canal. It is contemplated spending $100,000,000 or more upon this work. To what end? Cheapening the cost of getting the output of the west to the seaboard. The government is being pressed to take over the control of the elevators at the head of lake Superior; to cheapen the Welland canal; to press along the construction of a line to Hudson bay; all these to what end? Cheapening the freight rate to the seaboard. To what use, if all control over or regulation of the carriers' charges is to be lost the moment the traffic reaches that point? A road to Hudson bay must and will be built. Take Regina as a central point for the shipment of grain and cattle to a Hudson bay port; control over the rates and facilities would exist for about 800 miles, and no control for 3,000 miles upon shipments to Liverpool.
Contracts have been let for the construction of elevators at Vancouver, and within a few years vast quantities of wheat from points as far east as Regina will find their way to the English consumer via Vancouver to Salina Cruz, thence over the Tehuantepec railway (189 miles) to Puerto, Mexico, and thence to Liverpool. The distances over this route are, Regina to Vancouver, 1,127 miles; Vancouver to Salina Cruz, 3,054 miles; Salina Cruz to Puerto, Mexico, 189 miles; Puerto, Mexico to Liverpool, 4,800 miles. Here is a rail haul of 1,316 miles, 1,127 in Canada, the rates over which are under control, and 189 in Mexico, and a water route of 7,854 miles. It is likely no effective control over the portion of this route through Mexico could be worked out; but the portion between Vancouver and Salina Cruz could be-probably the portion of the route between Puerto, Mexico and Liverpool could-as to all grain shipped from Canadian ports- also be brought under a controlling tribunal.
After the completion of the Panama canal Canadian grain from British Columbia ports will go all water to Liverpool the distance to which from Vancouver is, via the Panama canal, 8,800 miles, and the rates over the whole of this route could be controlled, apart from canal tolls, if any.
All that has been said about the movement of grain applies to all traffic moving from Canada to Great
Britain, and with still greater force upon all traffic coming from there to Canada, because if from an interior point the rail route there is so much shorter than in Canada.
Applications are continually made to the Board of Railway Commissioners for reduction in freight charges upon export traffic, such as cheese, butter, bacon, cattle, grain and so forth, and every reduction made on the land haul gives the ocean carrier an opportunity to add that to his charges. In a few years' time frort 600,000,000 to 800,000,000 bushels of wheat alone will be exported from Canada to Great Britain, and with all the	return traffic	that	such an	exportbusiness means it	will be a sorry day for the	peopleof Great Britain and Canada if it is to be left to the ocean carriers to say what they are to be charged for the	ocean portion	of	the route.	The
time to obtain control over the rates upon this traffic is while it is comparatively in its infancy, and not after enormous development has taken place and shipping trusts of all kinds have grown up. Had the United States established a railway commission thirty years before they did, they would never have had the abuses they have, since its establishment, been endeavouring to cure.
Express traffic is increasing rapidly.	There are
demands from all over Canada for reduction in express tolls. Take this illustration-a package is sent from England to Winnipeg by the Dominion Express Company, which	is owned by	the	Canadian	Pacific
Railway Company. This package comes over the Atlantic in a Canadian Pacific Railway steamer to Montreal; thence over the Canadian Pacific railway to Winnipeg. What is the use of reducing the toll from Montreal to Winnipeg when all the express company requires to do is to increase the ocean toll to take up the difference? The same may be said of practically all traffic between the two countries to-day.
An international tribunal, consisting of the English Railway and Canal Traffic Commission and the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, or certain defined members of these commissions, could, by joint legislation, easily be empowered to control all these matters. Many details would have to be provided for, but there is no doubt acts could be framed applying the general principles of railway rate controlling legislation to ocean carrier. They are in effect common carriers. Most of them are incorporated in Great Britain or Canada. Very large sums are annually expended for their benefit in harbour improvements, lighthouses, buoys and	so forth.	They	may easilyform monopolies; it is charged that they have many times done so. Great Britain is dependent upon her food supply from abroad. This supply will increase yearly from Canada. The imports to Canada from there will increase yearly; so surely it is in the interests of the people of both countries that the ocean rates upon all this traffic should be under some controlling tribunal.	Nor	should it	be to	the disadvantage of the	ocean	carrier.	Recently rates onwestbound traffic	were	increased	25 per	cent; the
carriers said they were losing money; the shippers raised much complaint. No means exist for ascertaining if this increase is proper. If ocean carriers were compelled to file tariffs and could be brought before a tribunal to show the necessity for increase, if the increase were proper it would be allowed; in which event there should be no dissatisfaction. As it is, the carriers may be compelled to increase rates, and thus incur much adverse criticism, notwithstanding they are in the right. If, on the other hand, they are in the wrong, some power should exist to control them.
This is a memorandum sent me by the late chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, Mr. Justice Mabee, and if I re-
