And I must read another letter by Lord Crewe to Lord Grey, in reply, I presume, to Lord Grey's communication which I read a few minutes ago. It reads:
With reference to my despatch No. 224 of the 31st of March, and to Your Excellency's despatch No. 90 of the 28th February, I have the honour to transmit to you. for the information of your ministers, the accompanying copy of a letter from the Assistant Secretary of the Marine department of the Board of Trade expressing the views of the board on the proposal to establish a joint tribunal for the regulation and control of ocean rates, together with a copy of the report of
the Royal Commission on Shipping Rings to which reference is made by the Board of Trade.
2. Your ministers will see that the board discover difficulties in the establishment of a joint tribunal for the regulation of ocean freights but suggest that there might be a discussion of the question of holding a joint enquiry into the rates charged and facilities afforded by the shipping companies engaged in the United Kingdom-Canada trade. You will no doubt furnish me in due course with the further observations of your ministers upon the question.
I have, etc.,
Crewe.
Hon. members having heard this, I wish to read to the House the amendment of the opposition. Mark you, we asked in 1910 for a joint tribunal. It was refused, the reason being given that it was impracticable. If it was impracticable in 1910, it is more so now, because the ramifications are greater. It was admitted by Mr. Grigg that there was a combine on the Atlantic, and as proof of that combine, he cited the fact that when the Elder-Dempster line had been sold to a member of the North Atlantic Steamship Conference, rates went up by leaps and bounds. He named the commodity and be asked, as representing the British government, that something be done. The government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, through a letter addressed by myself to the then head of the Board of Railway Commissioners, outlined a proposition. I have read the reply which, to put the case mildly, was an absolute refusal to have a joint board. What does the amendment of my hon. friend say? This is the amendment of the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark), speaking for the opposition:
I therefore move that Mr. Speaker do not now leave the chair, but that it be resolved: That effective control oif ocean rates can be exercised only with the co-operation of all portions of the empire, and by a body on whioh all are represented, aind the contract made by the government with Sir William Petersen, based on the report of W. T. R. Preston, is ill-advised-
And so forth. This amendment asks us in this parliament in the Dominion of Canada as representatives of the people to pass a resolution requesting the British government to do something which they refused to do in 1910. Is that going about the matter in a practical way? I can tell hon. members now my private opinion of what it is worth, namely, that this country will never get any control over ocean rates foy a combination made up of the different parts of the empire. We are here to look after the interests of the Canadian people, and if this plan that is now proposed fails, this government is going to endeavour to get some other plan that will not fail. I say it advisedly again that there can be no efficacy in this amendment which asks the British government to form a body,
Ocean Shipping Rates

which the British government was asked to form years ago when the situation was not nearly as acute as it is at the present time, and which that government refused. Great Britain is greatly interested in shipping. It controls to a large extent the shipping of the world, and I say this not with any prejudice, that the great mass of the people in Great Britain are interested in the success of the greatest industry they have, that is shipping, and they are not interested in the decrease of the rates which that shipping gets.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Will the minister say, as regards the document that he read embodying the policy of the British government, whether this is the first time it has been published?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I am not sure, but this
is the first time I have published it. I have been asked: The British government askdd for a reply to your last document, what reply did you make? I made no reply whatever. I know when I am turned down.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Has this document
been on the departmental files ever since?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: This document has been with the Board of Railway Commissioners and I have been digging assiduously for a few days to find out things. My memory served me fairly well as to where these things were, but I wanted the documents themselves. I have been asked, as I said before, what reply I made when the British government asked for a reply to their document suggesting an investigation. I made no reply so far as I can find, and I think my memory serves me well at the same time, because we were after something to control ocean rates, not something to investigate. We had the proof from different parts of Canada, from our shippers, that they thought ocean rates were too high, and we wanted to devise some scheme to control ocean rates, as I outlined this afternoon. We did not need any further investigation. I say frankly that I considered the suggestion to make further investigation just another method of side-stepping the whole question and getting away from the one thing we were after.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Why did you not reach for the big stick?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: We think we have one now.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Preston?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite are investigating Preston all the time instead

of investigating ocean rates. I am trying to stick to the subject.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Why did the minister send him over if the minister knew all about it before?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that his friend the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) would have been out of a job if we had removed Preston from the scene. I am going to stick right to this text of mine because it is very illuminating, and my hon. friends will discover that they were in it up to their ears and were endeavouring to do the same thing in their minds. The British government refused to appoint a joint board. We say now that it is futile, foolish, to fish out an amendment asking them to do something which they have refused to do and which this House knows they have refused to do.
But all the virtue was not in the Liberal government. Occasionally there are spasms of lucid intervals with our friends. When the people of Canada, through a misconceived notion, changed governments, the successor to Mr. Justice Mabee had the same idea that Mr. Justice Mabee had, that there should be some way of controlling ocean rates in line with the authority and machinery provided for the control of rates by land. So, the hon. member for IVest York (Sir Henry Drayton) very wisely, and I will not say following up what his predecessor did, but following along the same line, came to the conclusion that some method should be devised to control ocean rates. The hon. member for West York and I discussed the matter in a friendly way several times. The government of that day, through an order in council, sent the hon. member for West York, then head of the Board of Railway Commissioners, to London, to see if he could accomplish something. I will read the order in council authorizing him to proceed. This is dated July 23, 1943. That was before the war:
The committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 15th July, 1913, from the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs, with reference to the question of the regulation of ocean freight rates.
The minister observes that this subject engaged the attention of the Canadian government in 1910. On the 26th February of that year a minute of council was passed advising that this matter should be brought to the attention of His Majesty's government with a view to the establishment of a joint tribunal for the regulation and control of ocean rates. In the month of August following, a despatch was received from the Secretary of State for the Colonies enclosing a memorandum from the Marine Department of the Board of Trade in which it is set forth that:-
" There seems no reason why His Majesty's government should not discuss with the Canadian government the question of holding a joint enquiry into the

Ocean Shipping Rates
rates charged and the facilities afforded by the shipping companies engaged in the trade between United Kingdom and Canadian .ports, either on the lines of the recommendation of the Royal Commission or on the lines of the enquiries provided for in the Combines Investigation Bill which it is understood has passed through the Canadian legislature."
It does not appear that any action was taken upon this suggestion.
The minister, conceiving the time to be opportune for renewing the consideration of this important question, recommends that H. L. Drayton, Esquire, Chief Commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners, be authorized to proceed to England for the purpose of discussing with .the Imperial authorities the question of governmental control of the charges made by the shipping companies to the public for the carriage of ocean-borne freight.
The committee, concurring, advise that Your Excellency may be pleased to forward a copy of this minute, if approved, to the Right Honourable the Secretary of State for the Colonies for the information of His Majesty's government.
All of which is respectifully submitted for approval.
Rodolphb Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
Ijp to that time we were all of the same mind; it did not need any Preston report nor the report of any committee to convince the government of 1911 as well as the one succeeding it that something ought to be done with ocean freight rates. And they sent the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) overseas to look into the matter. I saw the hon. gentleman the day he was going and he was full of enthusiasm, but I suggested that he would come back with the same information that I already had. He went over and did his best, and I am not going to discuss anything that occurred or did not occur. But no board wras formed for the control of ocean rates, nor has there been any up to this day. I want to be fair, and I will observe that there are difficulties. As has been pointed out, the ocean is not like the right of way of a railway; if you make it too hard for ships to come to one port they can go to another. The difficulties therefore are great. But it does strike me that if Canada had had the sympathy of the British Board of Trade, part of the British government, in endeavouring to arrange fair ocean rates, a tribunal could have been established that might have had some effect at least. And the very fact that a combination had been formed from various parts of the empire, having in view the control of ocean rates, would have had the effect perhaps of obviating any necessity for action at all looking to the control of rates.
The question has been asked, and I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is somewhat enthusiastic about it-Why do you not use the merchant marine? Well, I will answer that question in due course. But before I take it up I want to refer to another matter, because I do not want to attribute anything to my right hon. friend's government which should properly be attributed to that of his predecessor. I find some correspondence tabled the other day, and in it there is a letter from Sir George Perley to the right hon. the Prime Minister of that day, now leader of the opposition, pointing out that excessive ocean rates exist, or at any rate that the people believe they exist. Let me read the first paragraph:
London, S.W., 4th January, 1921. Dear Mr. Meighen,-You will remember that during the past ten years the question of ocean freight rates has been discussed many times, as they often seemed higher than wa3 reasonable, and some of us thought that a way might be found for controllng them by a body similar to our railway commission. I am sure that you have been approached many times on the subject and I had occasion to look into it a good deal when carrying on the Trade and Commerce department in Ottawa in Sir George Foster's absence. Not long after we came into power, while Acting Prime Minister, I arranged with Sir Henry Drayton to come over here and try and find out the feeling here on the subject.
Now listen.
He came back not feeling very hopeful about the possibility of getting anything done in the direction of freight rate control but he will be able to tell you about this himself.
The reading of that confirms what I have stated. The second attempt, yes, the third attempt did not get us anywhere, no matter what party was ini power on this side of the line.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: What was the third attempt?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
This is the third attempt about which I am reading now. To proceed: Nothing was done about this question during the war but on April 29, 1919, I received the following cable from Sir Thomas White who was then Acting Prime Minister.
Sir Thomas White evidently thought there was need of action. I am just reading portions of the letter.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
It is not long and hon.
members would like to have it all.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Very well, I will read it.
Canada much concerned about ocean freight rates- Enquire and cable whether British government would co-operate with Canada in giving effect to report of Royal Commission on Natural Resources, Trade and Legislation of certain portions empire as presented to Imperial parliament in March, 1917-this report finds that it is not desirable that operations of steamship companies carrying passengers and freight between Canada and England should remain longer without government supervision-most important to obtain official position of British authorities respecting matter." This I at once communicated to the Colonial Secretary here and I spoke to Sir Robert Borden about it when I was in Paris a few days after receiving it. In the reply from the Colonial Office they drew attention to a despatch which had been sent to the Gov-
Ocean Shipping Rates

ernor General on December 9. 1918, and which contained suggestions for the constitution of an Imperial Investigation Board for the purpose of reviewing questions relating to maritime transport and to the development of the sea communications of the empire.
Sir Robert Borden had evidently been giving the matter his careful consideration and in May, 1919, he prepared a memorandum "respecting necessary control of ocean freight rates and the disposition of available shipping", of which you will find a copy attached. This memorandum, which suggested in effect that the control of ocean rates and disposition of shipping should be placed in the hands of a commission, composed of representatives from the various parts of the Empire, was transmitted to Mr. Lloyd George and to the Prime Ministers of the other dominions.
Canada had acquiesced in the suggestion for the appointment of the Imperial Investigation Boad but in view of Sir Robert Borden's memorandum further consideration was given to the matter and eventually the Imperial Shipping Committee was created on the lines of the Colonial Secretary's despatch to the Governor General of Canada of October 11, 1919, by an instrument under the hand of Mr. Lloyd George dated June 15, 1920, copies of both of which you will find attached.
As the question of the control of freight rates had been one of much interest to Canada I rather felt that, if it were to be taken up seriously before this committee, someone with technical knowledge and understanding of commercial shipping questions should be here to assist me in my capacity as the representative of Canada on this committee. I put my views forward fully to Sir Robert Borden in a letter dated December 9, 1919, and, after this had been considered at Ottawa, Sir George Foster wrote me suggesting that Mr. William Phillips, who is the European manager over here for the Canadian National Railways, might act in the capacity of an adviser, on account of his knowledge of Canadian conditions and of shipping matters in general. I arranged with Mr. Phillips accordingly and he has been both courteous and helpful. I took him with me to the first meeting of the committee and I arranged that he could attend in my absence, although he is of course a busy man. Yesterday we had a long talk on the subject and reviewed the position as it has developed so far. The committee has held some 14 or 15 meetings, of which six have been devoted to "Ship-owners' liability by clauses in bills of lading", and the majority of the others to evidence given by representatives of various port authorities on questions relating to port facilities, control and development.
On July 29 last the chairman of the committee wrote me (copy of letter enclosed) saying that the committee desired to be furnished with up to date information regarding dock and harbour accommodation and other maritime transport facilities and would be glad to have before them as full a statement as possible of the views of the Canadian government on the questions falling within the scope of the terms of reference.
This letter was referred to the Department of Marine in Ottawa and I have a reply from them saying that the information asked for is being prepared and will be forwarded shortly, but that, so far as they know, the Dominion government has no statement to make.
The reason that I am writing you at the present time is in order that you may consider and decide whether you wish to bring' before the committee the question of the control of freight rates. I understand that this was the chief ground on which the Canadian government favoured the appointment ^ of the committee, but this question has so far received but slight attention, as the committee has occupied itself mainly in the discussion of subjects which, while no doubt important, have but little bearing on this point.

Let me interpolate, that that will be the result of every meeting you have of a committee of that kind: it will discuss everything but the question of ocean freight rates.
The terms of reference do not definitely give the committee authority to consider the possibility of controlling freight rates, but I explained fully to the committee at their first meeting the interest which Canada took in that question, and that it was largely in view of Sir Robert Borden's memorandum on that point that the committee had been created. The instrument of appointment gives the committee authority to inquire into and report " on all matters connected with ocean freights and facilities," which appears to be sufficiently broad to cover the question of control of freights.	_
Then you will see that one of the clauses in Sir Halford Mackinder's letter of July 29 is as follows:
" If your government should think it desirable now to nominate witnesses the committee would be glad to have information as to when they would be available to give evidence." The present therefore would appear to be an opportune time to take up with the committee the question of the control of ocean freight rates if you think it advisable to do so. I realize quite well that the position is not quite the same now that it was before the war. In the first place, there is at the present time a plentiful supply of ships and therefore freight nates naturally tend to adjust themselves on a reasonable basis. Then there is of course the fact that the Canadian government now owns quite a large number of ships and is therefore in that way able to exercise a certain amount of control regarding rates. These facts may influence the views of the government on the subject, but in any case I -would suggest that the question be considered and a decision arrived at as to whether you care to press the matter before the Imperial Shipping committee on the basis of the memorandum prepared by Sir Robert Borden in May, 1919. If you should decide to do this, I think you will agree with me that someone with full technical knowledge and who understands commercial shipping questions should prepare the Canadian case carefully and then come over here to appear before the committee and to give evidence regarding it. As such a large amount of tonnage is owned in these Islands they are perhaps naturally not very anxious about the control of freight rates and therefore, if you decide to bring the question before the committee, I do not think it possible to give too much time or attention to the preparation of our case.
Will you kindly consider this matter and advise me as to your wishes.
Yours sincerely,
George H. Perley.
Now, if I had read that letter in the first place it would have saved a large portion of my speech, because Sir George Perley, in mild language, absolutely states the case as it is, that there is not much sympathy in Great Britain for the practical control of ocean rates. It is so simply on the face of it.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Does the minister mean to tell us that the manufacturers of Great Britain have no particular interest in low ocean rates? Have they not just as much interest in securing low rates as the shipping companies have in maintaining high rates?

Ocean Shipping Rates

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I would not go that far.
But there are so many of them and so few of us. As a matter of fact, the greatest industry in Great Britain is shipping; the success of Great Britain depends largely on the profits of its shipping, and from the government down most of the people are shareholders in the shipping companies of Great Britain. In a word, the vast majority of the people have, directly or indirectly, investments in the shipping of Great Britain, and on the success of that shipping depends to a large extent the industrial prosperity of Great Britain. They are not like we are in Canada at all.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I was wondering whether the
minister had considered the possibility of the British government retaliating against the proposal of the Canadian government, and what would be the result of such retaliation?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: How would they retaliate?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: After reading the British debate on the Petersen contract it seemed to me that Mr. Guinness had already fired the first shot, and that that might be the ominous beginning of war between the British government and our own.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I would not have such a
poor opinion of the British government as that. Of course we have in this country people who would retaliate to the limit against the United States on the tariff, but a good many of us think that that action would not do us any good. I am not inclined to think there would be any retaliation. On the contrary, I fancy Great Britain rather likes to see her sons overseas show a disposition to look after themselves.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I am not suggesting any such
strife, but it is a point that has troubled me considerably, and I was wondering if the minister could forsee its probable consequences. As he says, the shipping profits are very vital to the public of Great Britain, and it is therefore only natural that the government should rally to the defence of the shipping interests. When the British government withdrew the subsidy to the Petersen firm, it seemed to me indicative of a possible development of strife between the two governments.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
We cannot foresee what
will happen, but I do not imagine that the British government in all its might would endeavour to crush out the Dominion of Canada's trade, because the trade of Canada is as 73
vital to Great Britain as the trade of Great Britain is to Canada, and Great
9 p.m. Britain is not likely to overlook the British preference in our tariff. But we have to look out for ourselves so far as we can. Let me refer for a moment to the supposed action of the British government with regard to Petersen. It has been said that the withdrawal of the British subsidy would prevent Sir William Petersen from going on with his contract with us. He says not. But if Sir William is prevented from doing so, he will not get a cent, and it will not cost us a cent. But we are going on in an earnest endeavour to bring about a state of affairs that will let the shipping companies of the world on the Atlantic and the Pacific know that Canada wants to get a square deal for her people.
Now, here is a letter, dated February 16, 1921, from the right hon. leader of the opposition, who was then Prime Minister:
Dear Sir George Perley,-After consideration of your letter of January 4, we have decided that the question of the control of ocean freight rates should be placed before the Imperial Shipping committee at an early date. We also agreed with your suggestion that the case from the Canadian viewpoint should be carefully prepared, and Dr. Magill, of the Grain Exchange, Winnipeg, has been asked to undertake the task. As soon as his report and recommendations are received they will be considered and transmitted to you for your guidance.
I understand Dr. Magill did not undertake the work.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: There was a letter asking him to undertake it.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
There was also a reply
from Dr. Magill, but apparently the government cannot find it.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Dr. Magill sent a telegram the other day stating that he had made no report. I would imagine he sent an acknowledgment of the invitation.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: It was in the correspondence.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
There we are right up to
1921 and not a blow struck for reduced freight rates. I think the correspondence I have read from Sir George Perley himself is absolutely convincing that no relief is to be expected in control of ocean rates through co-operation of the various parts of the empire, without anything I have said being taken into consideration at all.
Now I come to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. It has been asked: Why do you not use the merchant marine? My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition in
Ocean Shipping Rates

his interruptions this afternoon intimated that that ought to be the course to be pursued. Let me refer 3rou again to Sir George Perley's letter. Sir George Perley in pointing out the difficulties of this ocean control, called the attention of the then Prime Minister, the present leader of the opposition to the fact that they now had a merchant marine in Canada that could in a measure control the rates. Why did they not do it? I notice that no one is speaking too loudly. The opposition ask-and those who have given the least study to it ask the oftener-why we do not use the merchant marine for this purpose now? Well, my right hon. friend, as was pointed out to him by Sir George Perley, had a brand new merchant marine, with the paint not yet dry on it-the ships being turned out; not a trade route established the removal of which would embarrass anyone-ships out there at anchor. And Sir George Perley was saying: "Why do you not put them to work to bring down freight rates?" But it was not done.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: They were all running.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Some of them were not finished until quite a while after the war. But here were these boats, free to be turned loose on the north Atlantic to reduce rates; and when the high commissioner asked the Prime Minister of the day to do it it was not done. They belonged to the north Atlantic conference and they were put on other routes; they were not used to break the freight rates on the north Atlantic. Now we are asked why we do not do it. There are two or three reasons, and I may help my right hon. friend out of the hole a little before I get through.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: I am not in it.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Badly. It is a great thing to feel happy-

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: I am glad I am not in the government's hole.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
And my right hon. friend
will not be for ,a great many years. At present the merchant marine ships are on established routes, that is, the ships that are capable of carrying large cargoes at reasonable rates. This government came in and found these ships. We were not responsible for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine which cost three or four times as much as it would now; but there the ships were, with a heavy capital expenditure, .and they had been handed over to the Canadian National Railways just a short time before. They were not in charge

of the minister who built them; Ithey were shifted over to another department. Unfortunately I was put at the head of that department. The management of the Canadian National Railways have been sending these ships over different routes throughout the world, getting away as far as possible from keen competition, because they could not in some circumstances compete with the faster ships or ships better adapted to -certain cargoes. New trade routes have been worked out that are of benefit to the Dominion of Canada. I asked one of the members from British Columbia !the other day, when he was talking about taking the ships off routes that were not paying-he did not say anything like that in 1921 when there were practically no routes established-I asked him if he would allow us Ito take the ships off the route that had been established between eastern 'Canada and1 Vancouver, and he immediately said no. These ships at the present moment are not paying but we are developing an interprovincial trade by water to the benefit of both extremes of the Dominion of Canada, and in a short time I believe they will bring a profit to the merchant marine as well as great good to the country.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: If the minister will allow me, I suggest that he may develop the ends and choke the centre through the custom house regulations at New York.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Now my hon. friend is running away to the Customs department. These ships do not need the Customs department. My hon. friend would want us to ship goods via American bottoms to New York. Well, we are trying to develop an all-Canadian route with the merchant marine that does not have to go to New York.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the minister, but I would remind him that I myself advocated last year just such a service as he is now speaking of, and it was advocated by others also. It was promised by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) who is unfortunately not in his seat. But will the minister tell the House when this service between Vancouver and eastern Canada by water was established? I understood him to say it had been established; am I correct?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: When was it established and what does it consist of?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I am not prepared to give those details. But it is carrying all the traffic that is offered and is prepared to increase the number of sailings as the traffic increases.

Ocean Shipping Rates

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: When was that service established?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Some months ago.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED

speechtext: I would not say that My hon. friend can say it if he likes. We are trying to establish-

speechtext: I do not want the minister to misunderstand me; I am only asking for information with regard to the service that my hon. friend is referring to. Of course, if he does not want to give the information, all right.

You come back to me and say there is no combine; I say I do not care whether there is a combine or not: Are the freight rates too high? I want to say before I sit down that I do not care whether there is a combine or not; that is not the question before this House. You would think to hear some hon. gentlemen speak that the question before the House was "Who is Preston?" "Who is Petersen?" "Has anybody got a combine?" The question before this House is first "Do we think the rates are too high on the ocean?" Everybody expresses the fear that they are. What is the cure? Somebody proposes the merchant marine though they never used the merchant

marine when they had it. Others say something else. The government, after a study of the case, believes this is one good plan to establish the principle of government control of ocean rates, and if it proves to be a success then the government will be prepared to proceed a step further. I make the prophecy before I sit down, that before this is all through, the leading shipping companies that sail the ocean will be prepared to make terms with the Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
The minister who has just taken his seat has been as interesting as he usually is, if not as convincing as usual. This debate has been conducted at very great length, and it would appear that it will go on for some time yet. The duration of this discussion would apparently indicate the importance of the subject. It is not only important because of the particular instance with which we are dealing. It is important for another and greater reason. Just as the last century witnessed a very keen competition, which in our present time has culminated in large combines and trusts, so the age in which we are living will witness efforts being put forward on the part of all governments in all countries to secure control over these combines and trusts, in order that the advantages which may be derived from combines may be secured to the people without allowing these combines to reap an undue reward at the public expense. It is because of the importance of the subject in this regard, as well as from the point of view that it actually implies the subsidizing of a private company without any very apparent reason, without any return from that operation, that I rise to speak on this question; also to explain the position that I and my colleague are forced to take on the issue; and further to present what I believe is a viewpoint that is, at least, a little different from any that has so far been put forward, whether that be a virtue or the contrary.
The first question to be considered is whether we have a combine or not. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals says it does not matter. Although the whole proposal has been based upon the assumption that there is a combine the minister now tells us that it does not matter whether there is one or not. But the government appointed a gentleman to investigate this matter and he has presented a report for the edification of members of parliament; a report which is calculated to demonstrate that there is a combine, and that the contract into which the government desires to enter is the way to break that combine. But I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I

Ocean Shipping Rates
have not come to the conclusion that there is a combine by the reading of the Preston report. If I were to take this report seriously, apart from the flat statement of the author, I would come to the conclusion that there is no combine at all. He says in one part of the report, quoting a letter from a manufacturer whose name he does not give:
I have representatives of the steamship companies calling on me every week, who are complaining about the small amount of freight that is offered.
He would have us believe that there are shipping companies in a combine and in a conspiracy against Canada; and that the agents of these companies in Montreal had been grumbling to the shippers because there was no freight for their empty ships. Surely this combine would not grumble over the lack of business, nor bring ships in hopes of obtaining a business that had been killed by its own design. Then if hon. members will turn to page 18 of the report they will find a table of figures which is supposed to show that very high rates have been charged against the Canadian and British trade, and particularly during 1924. This table is given to prove that .there is a combine and that that combine is engaged in a conspiracy against British and Canadian trade. He shows us by this column of figures that in 1924 the freight was very much higher to British ports from Canada than to ports in Europe. But if hon. members will turn to the column of figures in 1923 they will find that the situation is reversed, so that if Mr. Preston had issued his report in that year he would have had to have said "Yes, there is a combine but that combine is in a conspiracy against the European trade in favour of Britain and Canada." So that I think it was fortunate for the government that this report happened to be made in 1924. I do not conclude as to a combine on the strength of this gentleman's word.
There is another reason why I would doubt the existence of a combine, if I were to depend upon the information which this report gives or which the government has given, and that is the proposal that has been put forward to defeat it. That in itself would appear to argue that if there is a combine it is no't very well combined, and that it is noit very large, for the proposed ten ships would not break a very large combine. However, I believe there is a combine, first because of my understanding of the nature of the processes that have been going on for the last century in our industrial and commercial life. The competition which has taken place in the industrial and commercial fields has led inevitably to combinations of
fairly equal forces for mutual benefits. In other words, co-operation which has been adopted as the policy of the farmers of this country, which is adopted largely by the labour organizations of this country, has been adopted long since by large corporations in competition with each other. Yes, combines are the natural outcome of the processes which have been going on for the ladt century. But if we required any special evidence of this we Would have to go to the report of the Agricultural Conditions committee of last year or to the report of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). However, the minister has just assured us that they had sufficient evidence of the proof of a combine in 1910. If the government had that proof it is not clear to the House, and I do not think it will be clear to the people of Canada, why they, in 1924 appointed another gentleman to make another investigation of something of which they already had all the proof which they required. That is of course a minor point, but so far the government has carefully fought shy of dealing with that point and it would appear that there is some reason for thus evading an explanation beyond that which has been vouchsafed to the House. I conclude then that there is a combine.
The next question is, Should the combine be broken and its development arrested in this way? I hasten to answer that question emphatically in the negative, notwithstanding the apparent enthusiasm of the Minister of Railways. It is very true that the next step from a combine is a monopoly, but then monopoly is the fruit of the system that the government supports. It is the natural ripe fruit of the system which the Canadian government advocates, which is endorsed by modern civilization, and if we are not prepared to eat the fruits we should not be prepared to scatter the seeds. Monopoly is the next step after a combine, and a combine is the result of a competitive system. We cannot escape the fruits. We have to pick them. No little ten-ship organization of the Minister of Railways is going to set back the great tide of a century. It might sound well to say it, but sociologically, historically and scientifically it is absurd, and even if it were not an absurdity, it would certainly not be the policy to follow. Combinations represent progress. Let me just mention some of the things which may be effected through combinations. No one will deny that a combine will render to any country an improvement in service. In the particular case before us, that of shipping, it will result in a more regular service, in a
Ocean Shipping Rates

higher standard of service, and' it will also result in the elimination of duplication, and to that extent should lend itself to a reduction in freights. It will stabilize the whole enterprise. It will lead to a stabilization of rates and also to a stabilization of business, for if a business man has to buy large quantities of goods in Europe, and feels that the freight rates are so much to-day, may be twice as much next month, he is hampered in his business. But when he knows that freight rates have been thoroughly regulated, and that he can count upon them being in a stabilized condition it gives him more confidence in the conduct of his business. Then, a combine is conducive to a uniform rate to all merchants, thus giving the smaller merchants an equal opportunity with the larger merchants, and tends to develop trade in places where otherwise it would be impossible to have it developed. So I say that without some such arrangement as combinations, even in the case of shipping, the whole trade would be demoralized and shippers would not obtain good service, nor would workmen engaged in shipping have a living condition. The Minister of Railways recognizes this principle, or did recognize this principle when speaking this evening. He pointed out that it had been begun in western Canada, that the wheat pool to which he referred was the first step, a combination of farmers in the selling of their produce.
The next thing according to the minister as a step towards the reduction of the cost of living was the appointment of the railway commission, and the appointment of that commission was made in order that it might stabilize rates. Here are the two principles. He recognizes the combine principle and he recognizes the controlling principle, but not the Atlantic combine principle. If the government were to go out to meet the needs of the farmers in the west in so far as they would be met by the wheat pool, anid practise the same principles they are trying to practise in regard to shipping, what would they do? They would' go out and bonus some individual in Winnipeg to start a little elevator all by himself in order to break the wheat combine; but they did not do that. And the farmers had more sense than to do it; they formed a large combine to put the thing over, as they say in popular parlance. But when it comes to the Atlantic it appears the Minister of Railways forgets about the principle exemplified in the wheat pool, he forgets about the principle of controlling rates by commission such as was appointed1 by the government of Canada in respect to railways, and
[Mu Uvine.]
he says, "We are going to bonus some private company to break the rates for us. We are going to buy one of these individuals out of the combine to see if we cannot break the combine." I repeat that if he could break the combine it would be a very serious matter indeed. It would be turning back the wheels of progress, but as I have no fear of that occurrence, I do not require to express any fears in regard to the continuation of the evolutionary process; rather I would express fears for the government in undertaking such a proposition. I will deal later in my remarks with the method of control, all that I am contending for at the present time is that combines are necessary, combines are not necessarily evil; but combines cannot be broken, and even, if they could be broken it would be very bad business.
The next point is that the government has decided to break the combine. The government has decided to turn back the wheels of progress and has decided to accomplish the impossible. In this regard some hon. mejnbers on the government side have laid claim to *an amount of courage which should be credited to the government for this great feat. If there is any courage in this regard, that courage is certainly shown in the government risking its life on a policy so ill-advised. II think however that the lack of enthusiasm which has been so evident on the part of government supporters of this resolution speaks a great deal better for the government than the alleged courage does.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman explain how the government has risked its life? I thought that was just what it was taking care of.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
That is a very fine question, and I, perhaps, ought to take a moment or two to answer. The government, in my opinion, is risking its life in this way, that if the expenditure is permitted- and this seems probable-there cannot possibly come from it any return that will be visible to the Canadian people. If then this government has had the courage to dip into the treasury of an already overtaxed people for SI,350,000 annually to bonus a private company on the other side of the ocean, for which subsidy there is no return, that takes a little bit of courage. Of course I know this is not what it appears to be to the government. The government, I imagine, thinks that before the next election will be too soon to speak of the fruits of this investment; that it will be able to say to the westerners: Behold, we are the great little government

Ocean Shipping Rates
that went forth with the Preston report in one hand and with one million dollars odd in the other and challenged the great leviathan that controls the seven seas. That sounds fine in an election campaign. I do not know of anything that could sound better.
The next thing, I imagine the government think in this regard is this. They know perfectly well that freight rates are due to come down just as everything else is due to come down, and it is probable that by next fall there may be a drop in freight rates from perfectly natural causes. Then they will be able to say: Do you not see what we did? Do you not see what a little bit of courage has brought about? Did we not bring that large combine to its knees? Why, look at the freight rates! That may be the idea of the government. But after all, my faith in the common sense of the Canadian people is greater than to think they will give many votes on the strength of that. Again, we might be mistaken there. It is just possible that the government might be able to get this over once, but the reaping day is sure to come.
The government has decided to attempt this reactionary move and it claims courage in its attempt. But I should like to see the government try out its courage on something that is a little nearer to its hand. Has the government enough courage to break the combine on the Great Lakes? There is a combine right next door to it. Canadian ships are carrying Canadian goods to American ports more cheaply than they are carrying, them to Canadian ports, and this government, with its superabundance of courage and with the right to tax the people to get millions for an overseas company,-would it not show a little bit of courage in breaking that combine? I have been suggesting not the breaking of a combine, but the control of a financial monopoly in Canada. I have never seen any evidence of courage on the part of the government with regard to that question. We have a combine in Nova Scotia that this government or the government of Canada has helped to build by subsidizing to the extent of ninety millions of the Canadian people's money. That combine at the present time is a very serious menace to the life and happiness of a great portion of Ithe people of Nova Scotia, and calls have come time and again from those people for assistance, but the government seems to have no courage at all. Even the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) who, I am sorry, is not in his seat, lacks that courage which is claimed for his government, when that problem is put before
him. He says he can do nothing in that regard, no matter how much courage he may have secretly hidden in his bosom, because there is a British North America Act. And yet I notice that he is bringing into this House a bill which practically sets forth all that my colleague and I have ever claimed so far as the authority of this government is concerned in dealing with that condition in Nova Scotia. I will not quote that bill; the time will come for that; but I want to point out clearly that there is no evidence of this Courage which the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) wanted to claim for his government for having taken this step to subsidize the Petersen company.
But since the government has selected this particular feat as the exemplification of its courage, I want to examine it from two points of view. I want to ask something about the method that the government is employing, and second, what results might with reason be anticipated? If hon. members on the other side of the House argue that they are not trying to break up a combine but to control, then I would say that if the effort that they are about to put forth is going to be at all efficient, it can have no other effect than to break up the combine, because what they are going to do seemingly, if they are going to do anything, is to buy these ships and to reduce freight rates on these ships in order that they may reduce rates generally or, at least, reduce rates on that particular line. It will be agreed surely that unless they reduce rates all around, this scheme will be a colossal failure. But they can reduce rates all around only by forcing each shipping company back to competition in rates, and to go back to cutthroat competition in rates would mean the breaking of the combines, so that is really what they are trying to do. This is not desirable and it is not practicable. Let us look at the method further. I am opposed to the method because it implies granting a subsidy to private companies. There may be occasions when it might be permissible to grant a subsidy. Personally, I am opposed to the principle, and I am very much opposed to it in the case before us. Not only am I opposed to it as a principle, but I am opposed to it because of the past history of the application of the principle in Canadian life. Look for a moment at the subsidizing of the Canadian Northern. We subsidized and subsidized it until it fell into our laps, a culmination which, perhaps, was the best part of its whole history. But nevertheless, that for which we subsidized it never materialized. Then the subsidies which have been granted
Ocean Shipping Rates

to the Canadian Pacific, as was pointed out by some other hon, member, are now a futility in the Supreme court. Other instances of failures as regards subsidizing private companies, failures in the sense that they have never produced that for which the companies were subsidized, are too-numerous to mention. The principle involved in this method of subsidizing a private company and also the experiences which we have had by the application of such a principle are sufficient in themselves to condemn this resolution.
But what are the practical results which we may hope to get? I notice that the government supporters of the resolution have not had very much to say about that. They would rather leave that to fate. They appeal to the faith of the House with respect to what we may hope to reap from this outlay. But let me examine briefly the phase of the subject. I have so far pointed out that if the government were successful in securing the reduction of freight rates in the whole north Atlantic trade, it could be so only by breaking the combine, and to break the combine is a reactionary movement. All that any government should attempt in the case of a combine is to safeguard the efficiency in services which that combine makes possible, and to see to it that no monopoly shall operate at the expense of the people. But no government should ever undertake to break up that which natural laws have established. Let us follow this question further. It is not likely that the combine will be smashed, so that we need not worry very much on that score. But what are the likely results if this scheme is put into force? Certainly the world* combine is not likely to be beaten so easily. There are some 500 ships in the north Atlantic combine alone, and that is only a little brother. The whole world combine is involved, however, and is it reasonable to suppose that this combine, finding its existence threatened on the north Atlantic, will be absolutely docile and sit quietly by, making no attempt to protect itself? Why, ten ships could make no appreciable difference to the world combine, but the shipping companies see in the present effort a reactionary movement and it is only natural to suppose that they would take steps to oppose it. It is not likely, however, that the combine will sit quietly by. If the combine is as strong as Mr Preston and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), make it out to be, it will not stand by silently while its privileges are being wrested from it by such a small force as ten ships on the Atlantic. Is it not rather a strange situation in which we find ourselves 
at the present time? The government is asking us to spend SI,300,000 odd to break a combine which we are helping to maintain by retaining in it sixty of our own Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships, operating at a loss. The Canadian merchant marine ships, according to the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) are still in the combine, and the Prime Minister tells us that the combine is so strong that if our ships withdraw from it they will be swept from the seas. Now, if sixty ships cannot afford to withdraw from the combine for fear of destruction how can the government explain the possibility of operating ten ships independently of the combine? These are some of the questions which the government has carefully avoided even so much as referring to. It is possible that the Prime Minister in his undue sensitiveness on the subject found himself at a disadvantage in being called upon to speak rather hastily; but his words will be found in Hansard. According to him the ships of the Canadian merchant marine are in this combine which he is going to tax the Canadian people in order to break, and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine cannot withdraw from the combine with safety. If that is not an absurdity then I do not know what is. But that is the position which the government brings forward for the approval of parliament.
And here is another probable result which was suggested by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird). If this combine is as strong as Mr. Preston's report alleges and as the Prime Minister states, if it is so strong that we dare not take our own ships from beneath its protecting care, then is it not reasonable to suppose that the combine will say to the government and to Sir William Petersen, "Keep your ten ships for the Canadian trade and we shall wait until you have grown tired of trying to do business with them." How long would it be before the government, under these circumstances, would be wiring to the combine to come to the assistance of Canadian trade? What could ten ships do if all other shipping companies were to withdraw from Canadian trade? It must be borne in mind that the combine, according to the government, is world-wide, and therefore would be in a position to boycott Canada.
Now if the government will persist in its futile attempt to break up the north Atlantic combine, surely the most effective and the easiest way to go about it would be first of all to withdraw from that combine the sixty ships belonging to our national system, and to employ them in Canadian trade. I thought

Ocean Shipping Rates
we were going to get some information from the Minister of Railways as to why it is that use is not being made of the Canadian merchant marine in the Atlantic trade as a means of reducing freight rates. But did any hon. gentleman gather from the minister's remarks the reason for the ships of the merchant marine not being made use of? The minister says that this government is not operating them in this trade because the other government did not. That was the logic of his remarks. ' Time and time again hon. members on the government side have insisted that the merchant marine is not properly equipped for the Atlantic trade. That is the statement; but we know from the facts that a large number of these ships have both the carrying capacity and the speed, which are the two most important things in any freight carrying trade. Possibly they might need a bulkhead here or there or some alteration of a minor character, but these are not prohibitive reasons for not using the merchant marine. I suggest therefore that if the government is sincere in its efforts to reduce freight rates it should put the whole fleet of the merchant marine into the north Atlantic trade, and1 if necessary add ten more ships. If this were done some results might be obtained!. But the government may say that it would cost a great deal to do this; we might be told that the government would not in this event be able to balance the budget next year any more than they can this year if anything of the kind were done. Hon. gentlemen may argue that way if they will. The fact remains that the Canadian people will have to pay the bill in the long run whether a private company or the government itself undertakes the expenditure. In the case of the latter the people will at least have their capital at the finish, whereas if the present proposal is persisted in there will be nothing to show but the receipts of the Petersen company. But whether the government allows a private company to build these ships or whether it builds them itself, there will be no difference to the Canadian people, who in either case will have to pay for the ships, inasmuch as it will be out of the freight rates charged that the ships will be paid for. So that as a matter of fact the cost will be collected from the people no matter who builds the ships. Any excuse along that line is therefore not intelligent.
It is argued moreover that even if the freight rates cannot be reduced generally as a result of the Petersen fleet of ten vessels, there would be a reduction of rates on the goods carried by those ten ships. Let us grant this point for the sake of argument; let us assume
that freight rates on the ten ships will be lower than those generally prevailing. Well, that is the greatest success than can be hoped for from the venture. But is it characteristic of the Petersen company that they will enter into an engagement with the government or with anybody else for that matter to carry on a shipping business at a loss. It is not very likely. It is reasonable to suppose, then, that we are going to pay that company for all the services we are to get in return. I am going to assume that we pay them this million and three-quarter dollars annually, I am going to assume also for the sake of argument-being very liberal with a rather illiberal government -that we are going to get back in reduced freight rates $1,300,000. Now, what have we in return? We have been at all the trouble and expense of collecting $1,300,000 from the pockets of the Canadian people, passing it to the private company, and then collecting it again from the Canadian people in freight rates. And that is supposed to be a reduction in freight rates!

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: The hon. minister interjects that we are going to get two or three times that amount. I think if he will go over his figures a little more carefully he will discover that I have given the very highest possible return. Merely because 'he makes the assertion that we are going to get two or three times that amount is not at all conclusive so far as I am concerned, and 3 am confident that he will have to furnish much better evidence than he has so far adduced before he will convince the House that we will not give to the Petersen company dollar for dollar,-that inasmuch as we are only giving them $1,300,000, we will not get any more from them in return by way of freight rates reduction. That, then, at the very best is all that we can hope for, and it simply amounts to our taking a dollar out of one pocket, slipping it into the other pocket, and then trying to hypnotize ourselves that w-e have actually made some money.
