subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. minister would, and I hope before I get through he will have arrived at that opinion, to drop the resolution is one of the things I am going to urge the government to do. But for the present I am trying to show that the utmost to be expected from this proposal is the reduction of freight rates to some extent in connection with the ten ships that the government proposes to subsidize; there is no possible hope of any other result.
Ocean Shipping Rates

My next point is that while combines are the necessary outcome of the system under which we are living, monopolies must be prevented. Since we cannot turn back the wheels of time and progress by reverting to cut-throat, competition, as we would have to do if we followed the policy of the administration, we are forced to contemplate some method of controlling a combine so as to prevent it from becoming a monopoly. Now, let there be no misunderstanding so far as I am concerned. I am just as well aware as the government is that ocean freight rates are high; I am just as well satisfied as the government is that they might be a little bit lower; I am also just as well satisfied as the government is that the people of Canada, and particularly the people of the western provinces, are desirous of securing cheaper transportation rates-all these things are frankly admitted. Merely because I am opposing what seems to me from every angle to be almost an absurdity, and what certainly gives no promise of being anything but an utter futility, I do not want it to appear that I am content with the ocean freight rates as they are, I do not want people to imagine that I would welcome a great combine or a powerful corporation or a monopoly controlling freight rates, I am just as anxious to see rates reduced, perhaps a little more so than the government is; but the reduction desired can only come about by a control which will have to be much more authoritative and much more fundamental than anything that the government has so far suggested. The amendment which has been moved by an non. member of the official opposition (Mr. Clark) at least points in the direction of an adequate control. It is not as positive as I should like to see it, it is not as specific in regard to the time within which action should be taken as I should like to see it, it does not go as far as I should like to see it go; but it at least has a stronger appeal to me

and I think to my colleague (Mr. Woodsworth)-than the proposal which I have been criticizing. It will be apparent also to the House that if I had a better proposal- which I have the conceit to think I have- the rules of the House, so celebrated and so acceptable, prohibit me from embodying my proposal in an amendment to the present amendment. Consequently my colleague and I are in the position of having either to vote for what we believe to be an absurdity or at best a futility or for an amendment which does not go as far as we would desire. We are forced to vote for the amendment because it points towards a control which we believe to be the only practical solution. It may be that 
it will take a longer time to gain our ends if we take the course indicated by the amendment, but when such control is secured it will be efficient.
The Minister of Railways is very emphatic in his opinion that because an attempt to secure control of ocean freight rates by the co-operation of the dominions with the Mother Country in 1910 was a failure, that therefore it is going to be a failure now and forever more, and he predicts with a sweeping prophetic enthusiasm that nothing may ever be expected to come out of any such proposal. I want to be as enthusiastic and as sweeping in my prophecy that nothing will ever come out of this pigmy of a proposal brought forward by the govern-
10 p.m. ment. There are hon. gentlemen in this House who have protested in times gone by that they did not want to vote for a subsidy, and I hope that if they be led into voting for this subsidy they will remember the criticisms which they have directed against other hon. gentlemen in preceding parliaments who blundered in this regard. I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that ten years from now-yes, a shorter time than ten years-there will be hon. gentlemen in this House who will condemn us for having voted a subsidy for such a proposal as this.
Control of a world combine is only possible by a world force: that world force can only be secured by the co-operation of the nations affected to secure the alleviation desired. If that attempt fail, then we should have to think of some other way to effect our purpose. But we are told that although this method proposed by the government may not get very far, at least it is trying, yes, it is trying to do something, and at least it is immediate in its application. So far as I can see all that is immediate about it is the expenditure of $1,300,000. That is very immediate-more immediate than is comfortable for the people of Canada; but the reduction of freight rates is remote, and so far the government has advanced no vestige of reason calculated to interest anybody who has been thinking about the matter and to arouse in him the slightest hope that any very beneficial result will crown the enterprise.
Now it would appear to me that when we have admitted the existence of a combine and when we have admitted high freight rates, we will have to admit something more than that. This parliament, it seems to me, will have to admit that Canada, by virtue of her geographical position, by virtue of her climatic conditions, by virtue of the whole nature of her industrial life, must institute a different

Ocean Shipping Rates
kind of policy than the one that is being followed at the present time. The policy at the present time would appear to be a policy of shipping out of the country as much as we possibly can; if we have not ships to carry our goods ouit, pay somebody to provide ships for that purpose-rather than a policy by which we will be able to approach a little nearer to a condition of self support. I will not develop this point at the moment, because I anticipate there will be an opportunity later for dealing more specifically with a general policy for Canada. But I will say this: that if the government had half as much courage as some of its members claim it would come forward with a policy that would depend less upon the caprice of shipping companies on the north Atlantic and much more upon the intelligence and the industry and the economic ability of our own people.
Now, it is argued that we should let this Petersen contract go to a committee; that if the proposal only arrives at a committee, although it has no sense in it now it might perhaps become sensible then. That is the argument that has been adopted by some hon. members. I do not hold that opinion. I see no intellectual virtue in a committee. That, however, is not really the question. I want to make it very clear that we are not voting, as some hon. members seem to think, to investigate the whole question of freight rates and combines and the proposals which might be put forward as a result of the knowledge we might thereby gather; that is not the question before this House. The question is whether we are going to endorse a specific agreement no letter or word of which we are permitted1 to alter in any particular. I want to cite in this connection the position taken by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), a position which I took to be a very strong one and which that hon. gentleman will have to hold, it seems to me, since there has been no change in the situation since he made his speech. He says in regard to this very point:
A bill after it has had its second reading is accepted in principle, the principle of the bill is accepted when the House agrees to its second reading. So that parliament, having accepted the principle of the bill in this instance, the bill itself could not be subject to any severe modifications on the part of a special committee.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made some remarks in regard to that which I will quote If anyone objects to my interpretation of them. The interpretation which I put upon his remarks is simply this: That we can have a committee after the House has
endorsed the principle which the committee is supposed to decide upon, we can send for Sir William Petersen and some other people and some changes may possibly be made, provided that Sir William Petersen and the government agree to them. The idea was to hold out the hope to those who have taken a very strong position that if the matter went to a committee something better might come out of it. But I want to point out here that if the Prime Minister was really sincere in that position, the easiest way out of the difficulty is to drop the proposal entirely and bring in a new one which would embody what he proposes to be willing to grant. Then there would be no difficulty about anybody voting. We will all vote for an investigation, because we desire it; we will all vote for a method of reducing freight rates, because we need it. That is not the question however, the question is whether we are to give the endoisation of this House to the principle embodied in a document which no committee, which not even the House, has the right to amend. That, as I understand it, is the situation, and so far as I am concerned, -and I think I speak also for the leader of the Labour party (Mr. Woodsworth) in this regard-I shall not be able to vote for the government's proposal. I shall support the amendment.
There is one more point I want to note: Parliament seems to have a strange psychological reaction on some people. I am not now reflecting on any hon. member; I have no doubt that if we could "see ourselves as others see us" perhaps I would be noting my own psychological reaction instead of that of other people. But the fact remains that hon. gentlemen have stood up and made what seemed to be very excellent proposals with regard to the reduction of freight rates. I refer in particular to the outline of a scheme that was put forward in the House last evening by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Euler), which was to acquire the Canadian Pacific Railway and join it up with the Canadian National; to utilize the present merchant marine and to belt the world with our own lines of transportation. That was, to him, a better way; that was the real way; that was the way that he said we would ultimately have to accept. He also protested that he was not in favour of the principle of subsidizing. Yet, like many other hon. gentlemen, he said, in effect, "While I am not in favour of subsidizing; while I know there is a better way, I am going to vote for the subsidy-x am going to vote for a secondary way in which I have very little faith." That is
Ocean Shipping Rates

the strange psychological reaction which I have noticed. My own, may, as I say, come out in some other regards, but it is not going to come out in this. I am opposed to subsidies in general; I am opposed to this subsidy in particular; and I am going to vote against the resolution. If all hon. members who do not believe in subsidies and who do not believe in the ultimate rewards from this particular agreement, will do the same, then the Minister of Trade and Commerce will have to withdraw his resolution and obey the real 'will of parliament. That will, judging by the expressions of hon. members, would appear to be that a special committee should be appointed to make a complete investigation of the whole question of combines and ocean freight rates, and also recommend to parliament some practical scheme to control the shipping combine. But we cannot hope for this if we vote for the resolution.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the very important question that is now being considered by the House, and in doing so may I make one reference to the remarks of the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine). He began his address by asking if there was a combine in north Atlantic rates, and immediately gave his conclusion that there was a combine; and he left the impression that there was no proof, or nothing that we could base a conclusion upon, to show it, that there was a monopoly. I will refer to that a little later in my remarks when I touch upon an investigation that was made by the Royal Commission on Shipping Rings. But let me follow his logic a little further. He told us that it was a mistake, that it was turning back the wheels of progress to break combinations, to destroy combines; and in the next breath he chided the government for not trying to break the combine on the Great Lakes, for not trying to tear down the financial institutions of this country, and for not interfering with the trouble in Nova Scotia. I do not think, Sir, it is necessary for me to follow further the remarks of the hon. member for East Calgary.
Now, Sir, in approaching the discussion of this question I wish to review the history of efforts to deal with ocean transportation and to control freight rates during the years that have passed1 in order, if possible, to throw some light upon this very important subject. My colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals in his speech this afternoon and evening went fairly extensively into the attitude of the government of Canada on the matter and the correspondence which this 
government has had with the Imperial authorities. Perhaps I may be permitted to add to the information which he gave the House by reviewing, to some extent, the investigations that have taken place under different governments that were interested in endeavouring to get some measure of control in this matter. Because, Sir, the principle involved in the present arrangement is whether the Canadian government is justified in endeavouring to secure control to some extent over these rates. That is the undoubted principle involved although some hon. gentlemen have endeavoured to thrust that fact into the back ground and to lead (the discussion into other channels.
Now let us go back a few years and consider what investigations have been made. I think the first was undertaken at the instance of the British government in 1906 when they appointed a Royal Commission on Shipping Rings. That commission isipent neatly three years in investigating the matter and as a result of its inquiries two reports were presented, a majority report and a minority report. In brief the conclusions submitted in the majority report were that a conference existed and that it controlled freight rates in British shipping particularly in the north Atlantic trade; that although the conference was a benefit in many ways, nevertheless through its agency steamship owners were able to effect collective bargaining, a thing which they could not otherwise hope to arrange; and as a remedial measure it was suggested that the shippers and exporters from other countries should unite and form themselves into a counter combination so that they might be able to combat the influence of the shipping rings. The further recommendation was made that the board of trade should be empowered to endeavour to promote a settlement by conciliation where a conflict of interests existed between ship owners and the conference. In my opinion the suggestion for a union to bring about a counter combination was an utterly futile proposition, because it was impossible to unite in any such arrangement shippers and exporters from the other countries of the world from whom the shipping rings secured their traffic. I think those gentlemen knew the idea was impossible to realize when they suggested it; and the further idea to employ a conciliatory method was, so to speak, a case of damning with faint praise the proposition to exercise control.
The report of the minority not only confirmed the finding of the majority that there was a combine or conference but went

Ocean Shipping Rates
further and stated that an actual monopoly existed. I should like here to read a few clauses from the findings of the minority report to show just what conclusions were arrived at:
The conference system with the deferred rebate-* the natural evolution of a highly organized trade dealing with customers for the most part scattered or disorganized-has created on almost all the chief ocean routes a monopoly, the limitations upon which are in many cases illusory, and which generally tend to decline.
The minority also arrived at this conclusion:
It has been successful in raising or keeping up rates.
The public have, as a rule, to pay higher rates of freight than they would pay in an open market.
The system tends to inflate the amount of tonnage and consequently the amount of capital invested upon which interest has to be paid.
I want the House to notice particularly the latter conclusion because the condition to which it refers is partly responsible for the state of affairs from which we are suffering to-day,-the result of the control that has been exercised by unduly inflated rates has encouraged more than the required amount of capital to be invested in shipping lines and we to-day have more ships than there are cargoes available for them which the report states tends to decline. The minority report, as did the majority report, also recommended power to be given to the board of trade to try and bring about a settlement by conciliation. However, the recommendations reflect very much the viewpoint which is held in Great Britain, and which was so well referred to by the Minister of Railways in his speech, that we in Canada need not expect our interests to be looked after by the Imperial Shipping Committee, or any other body appointed by the British government in the matter of the contrdl of rates. There was a reservation in the minority report made by Sir David Barbour which I think is worthy of notice:
For example, it has happened in the past, and will happen in the future, that the members of a shipping ring have miscalculated the prospects of trade, and have provided more ships than the trade really requires or can employ.
In such cases there will be a very strong temptation to pass the loss on to the public and the existence of a monopoly affords an easy and convenient means of so doing.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the situation revealed by the extracts I have quoted resembles the very situation that we in Canada are in today: The ocean rates are high, and they are controlled and kept up by the influences behind the North Atlantic Steamship Conference, and they are kept up to a point which is necessary to enable those who are interested in the shipping companies to get
a return on an investment greater than the trade conditions call for. I will demonstrate that a little later on in my remarks. I think I have shown that the British investigations disclose that there is a combine or a monopoly, that it inflates rates to an undue figure, and that they are kept at that high point by the power which the combine is able to exercise through collective action.
I think it is only necessary for me to make a passing reference to other investigations in Great Britain. The inquiry made by the Dominions Royal Commission was referred to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in introducing the present resolution, and was again dealt with in considerable detail by the Minister of Railways and Canals in his speech to-night. I shall not repeat the statements of my colleague, but will content myself by mentioning one outstanding point which I think bears directly on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark). That is that in 1910 the British government refused to consent to any measure of control when asked to do so by the Canadian government, the British authorities suggesting further investigation. My hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton), who went to Great Britain two years later in the hope of finding the British government in such a frame of mind that they would consent at least to some measure of control, made a report. I have that report in my hand1 and I will read one or two sentences from it to show that really my hon. friend must have mellowed down when he was in the Old Country, because among other things he made a recommendation for further investigation. He said:
With this end in view I endeavoured to obtain the appointment of a joint commission to make a thorough and complete investigation of and to report on the methods and practices, and rates and charges of ocean carriers doing business or from time to time doing business, between ports in the United Kingdom and ports in the Dominion of Canada.
I further impressed upon the Imperial authorities that it was the desire of the Canadian government that the investigation should be entered on in the near future, and if possible a report made so as to enable any necessary action to be taken by that government at the ensuing session of parliament.
Hon members will see that after the British government had- refused to take action and wanted further investigation, the hon. member for West York fell in with their viewpoint, and so recommended when he came back to Canada. It is simply carrying on an interminable investigation, which is the object of the amendment moved1 to this resolution by our hon. friends opposite. I think, Mr. Speaker, that with the information in
Ocean Shipping Rates

the hands of the government, the time has come when people of this country desire that the government shall act with the precision and carefulness that are necessary in all matters of this kind. I wish to more fully emphasize the conditions that exist; because after alll, in facing this question, we must face it in the light of the answer to the question; does a condition exist such as we believe, and if so, have we any better method or proposal to suggest than that which is put forward by the government at the present time? I submit that up to the present, Mr. Speaker, no suggestion of a constructive kind has been put forward to take the place of the one proposed by the government. I do not think, after considering all the circumstances of the case, that any better proposal can be put forward by one of the overseas dominions acting alone than thq resolution at present before the House. Before dealing with that matter I want to cite to the House the result of an investigation that was held by the government of the United States in 1913. They were troubled, as Canada has ibeen, with high freight rates; they desired to keep the Atlantic clear for American commerce, and they felt the pressure of control exercised by the shipping companies, with the result that they referred the question to the standing committee on Merchant Marine pnd Fisheries of the House of Representatives at Washington. I will just read the reference made to the committee on the 18th June 1912:
That the committee be empowered and directed to make a complete investigation of the methods and practices of the various ship lines both domestic and foreign engaged in carrying overseas or foreign commerce, to investigate whether any such shipping lines have formed any agreement, understanding, working arrangement, conferences, pools, or other combinations among one another for the purpose of fixing rates and tariffs, or of giving and receiving rebates, special rates or other special privileges or advantages, or for the purpose of pooling or dividing their earnings, losses or traffic, or for the purpose of preventing or destroying competition.
That is the very thing in which we are interested in the proposal we are now considering in this chamber. This committee began their sittings in January, 1913, and took evidence from the steamship owners, from the commission merchants, from the exporters and business men along the Atlantic coast who were directly and personally interested in ^American exports and imports. I say further by way of explanation that I have not been able to find that the committee made a report to the House of Representatives, but they did submit the evidence for the consideration of the House, and I will cite a few of the

main paragraphs from the evidence thus submitted. Let me first refer to some evidence that was submitted1 by a gentleman in New York, with regard to the control exercised :by European lines over the American Brazilian lines. The gentleman who was giving evidence was Mr. Sydney Story, vice president of the Pan-American Mail Steamship Com-ipany of New Orleans. He said:
There is no doubt in the world that there is a great war being waged against the commerce of our country by our aggressive commercial rivals. When I was in Brazil last, negotiating with the government for aid to this American effort of ours from New Orleans, it was openly stated on the streets by the friends of the Euroipean lines who control the monopoly of transportation between North and South America that our line would not be permitted to exist; that we would be run out of the trade in from four to five months.
That is the evidence of a gentleman who was negotiating with the steamship lines trying .to make an arrangement between Brazil and the United: States. Further evidence was given by a New York agent of another Brazilian steamship company, Mr. Joseph J. Slechta. He said:
So, as regards most of the trans-Atlantic business, you must bear in mind the fact that Brazil has for one hundred years been very largely dependent upon the development of her commerce, entirely upon her foreign commerce, and if she were to discriminate, or to take any really very severe measures against these lines, their boycotting would hurt the country very seriously. And that is the situation with which they are confronted, although, I must advise the committee at this point that upon receiving your summons the other day I cabled the situation to my head office, and received the reply that their own government was taking steps to effectively put the combine out of business. I asked for further details, which I have not received, although I am momentarily expecting an answer about it.
That evidence shows two things which probably might be taken into consideration by us, and that is that Brazil had been struggling for many years, a hundred years perhaps, to overcome the effects of the unfair control thus exercised, and that the government in the end, after a hundred years of attempt, had to try to break the monopoly ,by granting a subsidy to other lines to come in and operate. Perhaps it would be interesting for the House to hear a little from the evidence of William Harris Douglas of the firm of Arkell & Douglas, exporters in New York city, who gave evidence stating very clearly his opinion in regard to a monopoly. Mr. Douglas said!:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Tell the committee what, if anything, you know about conditions of the trade-the relations between the ship lines with whom you transact business.
Mr. Douglas:	The American carrying trade, as we
all know, is monopolized by the foreign steamship owners. It is a combination of the English and Ger-

Ocean Shipping Rates
man and other nations. They have their established lines from our ports running in all directions, you might say, and they cover the world. These lines are largely in combination between themselves, and their ramifications extend to Hamburg and London, and they exchange their conferences in Europe, because there is the head and front of the combination in America, and the idea that the ocean is free is one of the fallacies of the American nation. The control of the ocean to-day, of all oceans, is a stronger and more pronounced and determined monopoly, you might say, than any intercolonial trade in our states; that is, by railroad or water transportations. They absolutely dominate the entire situation.
I might cite other evidence of that nature, but I have cited these extracts to show the tenor of the evidence given by those who are interested in American trade. Some of the commission merchants went on further to show how completely they were under the control of the combine, how trade was suffering, and also why, in their opinion, the government agency was the only power that could break this combine or take any steps towards doing so.
Another feature which we might note is in regard to the methods that were put forth by the steamship companies in the earlier days, ten or twelve years ago, to get control of the lines that were outside of the conference. Evidence is submitted here which clearly shows that there was an organized effort, and that wherever a line was put on to compete with the conference lines, fighting ships were sent in to carry freight at a lower rate. In the end these lines were put out of business or absorbed by the line which went in the first place to provide the fighting ships. By that method used in those years of driving any independent line into the conference or out of business, they were able to get control which extended its effects to the commerce of both Canada and the United States and, indeed, to the commerce of all overseas dominions and foreign nations.
There is further evidence given by leading shipping men to show that all countries had to assist their steamship lines by means of subsidies or money assistance in order to keep their channels of commerce free. I think I may briefly say that the result of the investigation by the committee of the House of Representatives at Washington was that the American government endeavoured to provide ships of their own, but it will be noted from the remarks that were made by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) this afternoon, and by following what was done by the American people with their merchant marine, that it has proved of no avail to control Atlantic rates with ships owned exclusively on this side of the water.
Perhaps I might say, just in passing, that another obstacle met by our merchant marine in trying to get control of Atlantic trade is the fact that the port facilities and harbours are controlled by those who control the Atlantic lines, and unless you get some measure of control in the Old Country you have very little effect in trying to fight the lines from this end. You cannot send ships over there and have them come back empty. Unless you get in with the shipping interests in the Old Country who control the ports, port facilities and brokerage houses, you have not much chance of getting freight coming back. We feel that in the proposal that is here offered that weakness will be overcome, by reason of the fact that the person with whom the contract is made is in a position to over come the weakness on the British side.
Let me say a word further in regard tc criticisms that have been offered as regards the merchant marine. We have been criticized from different parts of this House for not using the merchant marine to break the combine. I do not wish to give my opinion, but something has been said as to the suitability of the merchant marine for ocean traffic. I will show in a few minutes who benefit most from the proposal that is being put forward in getting control of rates. But first let me read the evidence which was given before the special committee of this House on agricultural conditions that sat in 1923 by a leading cattle broker in the city of Montreal, and I think his evidence will bear me out. This is the evidence given by Mr. Duncan A. Campbell of Montreal, who is a cattle broker and whose business it is, as stated in the evidence, to secure space and make shipments of cattle for his clients in this country:
Q. You have placed in my hands, Mr. Campbell, a statement of animals carried on board the Canadian Commander, the Canadian Hunter, the Canadian Trader, the Canadian Ranger, the Canadian Raider, the Canadian Victor, and the Canadian Rancher.-A. For the season of 1921?
Q. In the season of 1921 ?-A. Yes.
Q. There was in all carried 2,830?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. With a loss of 95, making a loss ratio of 3.35 per cent?-A. Yes.
Q. Will you tell the committee whether that is 8 large or small ratio?-A. I told the gentlemen here, that we can insure cattle-well, to go back a little further, that you may have all the information in connection with insurance. When, after the close of the war, I went to New York to get insurance, the best rate I could get was one and a half per cent. I was first quoted two per cent, but I succeeded in getting one and a half per cent. Afterwards, I got it down to one per cent, and then three-quarters. During the month of May and the early part of June last year, it was three-quarters. We then got a rate of five-eighths of one per cent. That is an all-risk policy, covering the animal from the moment he walks aboard the steamer until he walks ashore down the gangway on the other side. An animal whicv f- unable to walk
Ocean Shipping Rates

ashore on the other side is taken over by the insurance company and the shipper is paid the full amount of his policy. For instance, if the animal is insured for $150, the owner of the policy gets $150.
Q. The full amount of the policy?-A. The full amount of the policy.
Q. This is a heavy list then?-A. Yes, this is 3.35, and the other is .621.
Q. What is the matter, Mr. Campbell?-A. These are not good cattle carriers.
And I want the House to note particularly this statement:
The chief reason is that the decks on these steamers are three feet high, as high as this table. With a deck of that height, cattle are carried on both sides, cattle are placed on top of them, and there is no place that you can brace the deck to, because the deck fittings come over the side fittings, and when a wave strikes it, they smash, the cattle fall into the hold of the ship, or are knocked into the winches. In one boat we had a big loss; there was a big storm, and the whole upper deck load of cattle was washed overboard.
Q. They cannot be altered any way to make them suitable?-A. During the months of May, June or July, or the first of August, these would not be very suitable, but in a pinch they would do.
Q. Is there any practical way in which these ships of the government marine can be altered to make them .suitable for carrying cattle?-A. No.
The most important thing for many of our farmers, especially those of central and western Canada, is the cattle business; and what has been said in regard to cattle is equally true of other kinds of freight so far as the construction of these ships is concerned. Mr. Campbell went on further in his evidence to show that the type of ship built during the war was not such as could be used to good advantage in .the Atlantic trade owing to the large hatches and low sides. It is not necessary for me to go further into that question, but I think that the experience of the past few years, both on the part of the late government as well as on the part of this government, in connection with the management of the merchant marine, shows no hope of our
being able to control Atlantic freights through the operation of the vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
Something has (been said on the subject of open rates on cattle, grain and flour. I do not want to spend too much time quoting, but evidence was given before the committee on Agricultural Conditions by Mr. Cunningham which will be found on pages 220 and 221, showing that the rates on wheat, flour and cattle are agreed upon at .New York as well as by the liner committee at Montreal. You may call them open rates if you like, but the evidence is that none of those who sit in at the conferences change the rate without notifying the others, and the rates are not made public any length of time in advance. As a matter of fact, it is difficult to know in advance just what the rates are going to be.
Let me refer now to another phase of the subject, the necessity for Canada as an exporting country to have some measure of control over the rates. Our export; trade during the fiscal year 1924 amounted to $1,045,351,056, of which total the sum of $360,057,782 went to the United Kingdom.
